metadata.screening: Excluded photographic and selected sensitive object categories plus records containing sacred, secret, restricted, ceremon, burial, funeral, human remains, human hair or initiation. Keyword screening cannot replace human cultural review.

metadata.slwa_screening: Keyword-matched public historical photographs were screened to exclude selected ceremonial, restricted, custodial, funerary, human-remains, sexual-violence and nudity terms. Keyword screening cannot replace cultural review.

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate for Hippi, King of Teraicha
records.collection: Terry Chesher, Peter Henchman and Jenny Barnes collection
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped brass breastplate with a convex curved surface, engraved with text "HIPPI / KING of TERAICHA". It also has an emu engraved on the proper right side and a kangaroo on the proper left side in naive style. A linked brass chain is attached to the two top corners.
records.significance_statement:
The Terry Chesher, Peter Henchman and Jenny Barnes Collection comprises two Aboriginal breastplates engraved "WILLEY/KING/OF THYLUNGRA" and "HIPPI/KING of TERAICHA".

The Willey plate is significant for a number of reasons. It is engraved with images of a moon and sun in traditional heraldic form, providing a demonstrable link between European heraldic devices on coats of arms and the engraved designs on Aboriginal breastplates. Thylungra is a station established by the pioneering Durack family in south-western Queensland in 1868 and there is a likely link between them and this breastplate. A family history mentions a Willie several times and it is likely they are one and the same person. Nothing is known of the second plate which is engraved with a kangaroo and emu, the most common design elements on Aboriginal breastplates. They are depicted in a naïve style unlike others in the Museum's collection.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate for King Wanney, 1861
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped breastplate with an inscription reading 'King Wanney / 1861'. There is decorative engraving beneath the inscription and the breastplate has a hole at each end.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a crescentric brass breastplate with the inscription 'King Wanney / 1861' above a stylised landscape.  The cursive script used is unique amongst the breastplates in the National Historical Collection and the inclusion of a date is unusual.  

Breastplates are a tangible record of relationships between individual settlers and Aboriginal people around mainland Australia. They were frequently presented to recognise the 'Chief' or 'King' of a 'tribe', which was often an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. They also often recognise service, such as on a pastoral property. The National Museum holds the largest collection of breastplates in the world, most of which are the only known record of the life of the recipient.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate for Joey, Chief of Petraman
places: Petraman (Associated place)
records.description: Edmund Milne (1861-1917) was born in England and emigrated to Queensland with his parents 19 months later. He had had personal contact with Aboriginal people throughout his life, from when he was a small boy in Queensland and, from the late 1860s, in New South Wales. This contact may have led him to recording the names of Aboriginal people associated with particular objects in his collection, at a time when this was rarely done. Milne seems to have begun actively collecting Indigenous artefacts in the early 1880s and was still acquiring objects a few months before his death in 1917. His work with the NSW Railways (1876-1917) enabled him to meet a broad range of people who facilitated his collecting and associated activities like visiting Aboriginal sites. From at least the time he lived at Orange NSW (1906-1915), and later at Ryde (1915-1917), near to Sydney city, he displayed his collection at his home. In addition to a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts, Milne's collection included artefacts from the South Pacific and prehistoric implements from Egypt, France and England. In his will dated 12 December 1916, Milne bequeathed his “Anthropological collection” to the “first Federal Museum opened in the Federal Capital”. The collection remained at Ryde until early 1931 when it was acquired by the Australian Institute of Anatomy in Canberra. It remained there until the Institute's collections were transferred to the National Museum of Australia in 1985.
records.physical_description: A crescentric brass breastplate with a hole at the edge of each horn to attach a chain. Engraved on the anterior surface is 'JOEY / Chief of / Petraman'. An emu image is engraved on the left corner, and a kangaroo image is engraved on the right corner.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate for King Tommy of Waverney
places: Waverney, Queensland, Australia (Associated place)
records.physical_description: A crescentric brass breastplate with a hole bored into the edge of each horn for a chain attachement and the words, "King Tommy of Waverney" engraved across the anterior surface. There is an emu image on the left horn and an image of a kangaroo engraved on the right horn.
records.significance_statement:
The Errol Beutel Collection No. 2 contains a crescent-shaped brass Aboriginal breastplate (gorget) with the transcription, King Tommy of Waverney. Gorgets were military in  origin and were part of a suit of armour worn by medieval knights. The presenting of breastplates was instituted by Governor Macquarie in 1815 and was  a strategy used by Europeans to elevate an Aboriginal person to a leadership position, as tokens of gratitude for services such as tracking or guiding expeditions, for bravery or to those believed to be the "last living member of a tribe".  Said to be collected by a scrap metal dealer, the breastplate is crudely made, perhaps the work of an amateur craftsperson.  Unevenly sawn from a brass plate, the lettering of the inscription is cramped and unevenly placed and the emu and kangaroo are simple, naive figures. The style of lettering and design suggest it was made in the late nineteenth century. 
  
Waverney was a remote cattle station, now abandoned, near Windorah on the vast gibber plains of Queensland's Channel country.  The Indigenous tribes of this region were the Karuwali, Malintji, Kuungkari, Marulta, Bidia, Kulumali, and Kungadutji peoples.  Windorah was gazetted as a town in 1880 and Jundah, 80 km northward up the Thomson, was gazetted in 1883.  The original owner of Waverney was John Costello, however, around the turn of the century, the station passed into the hands of the Bowman family.  A report from Harold Meston, Protector of Aborigines for Queensland's far west, dated 14th June, 1902, lists Tommy (Goorkillee) and Tommy (Mooloojoolah) among the Aborigines who lived in this area. The Register of Aboriginal Deaths in Queensland (1910-1928), from Queensland’s State Archives, records the death, from old age, of a 'full-blood' Aboriginal man,King Tommy, in Jundah, on 26th July, 1914.  It is possible that this man was the owner of the breastplate in this collection.

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate presented to Jackey Lewis of Bathurst
places: Bathurst, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)
records.description: The Jackey Lewis breastplate is significant both due to its association with William Cox, who reportedly collected the object, and due to its documented provenance. Jackey Lewis was reported to be the 'Chief of the Bathurst tribes' by the Sydney Gazette and New South Wales Advertiser in January of 1832, and he was described as wearing the breastplate at that time. This would make the Jackey Lewis breastplate one of the oldest breastplates in the National Historic Collection.
records.physical_description: A crescent- shaped brass breastplate with a metal chain. The breastplate is engraved 'JACKEY LEWIS / Chief of the Bathurst Tribe'.
records.significance_statement:
The Jackey Lewis collection comprises a brass breastplate and metal chain. It is of the common crescent shape, and engraved with the words 'JACKEY LEWIS / King of the Bathurst tribe'.  The breastplate can be dated to around 1829, both by its design and by a newspaper report from the period, which describes Jackey Lewis wearing the breastplate.

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate for King Too Too, Crack Horsebreaker & Glastonbury Coach Groom
places: Gympie, Queensland, Australia (Place made)
records.physical_description: A rectangular brass breastplate with rounded corners, engraved "KING TOO TOO, / CRACK HORSEBREAKER / & GLASTONBURY / COACH / GROOM / W.H Lynn, Engraver" with an image of an emu to the left of the text and an image of a kangaroo to the right. The breastplate has rounded corners and there are holes in the top two corners for a chain or cord. On the reverse are the maker's details "Wm.H.Lynn / General / Engraver / Gympie / Jany. 1888"
records.significance_statement:
The Genevieve Head Collection comprises a rectangular metal breastplate inscribed 'King Too Too Crack Horsebreaker and Glastonbury Coach Groom'. There is an emu engraved at the lower left and a kangaroo at the lower right. The breastplate has rounded corners and there are holes in the top two corners for a chain or cord. On the reverse are the maker's details: W M Lynn of Gympie (Qld) 1888.

The breastplate was acquired by Ms Head's father, a skilled horseman himself, while serving with the Australian Army in Queensland during the Second World War. He returned to Western Australia after his discharge and it has been in the family ever since. The practice of awarding breastplates to Australian Aboriginals dates from 1830 and continued to the 1930s. King Too Too's breastplate is significant as it documents his skills as horsebreaker and groom. It also records more maker's information than many other breastplates.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.educational_significance:
This is an Aboriginal brass breastplate with a hole at the edge of each horn to attach a chain. 'Timothy / Chief of / Merricumbene' is engraved on the anterior surface. A raised, peaked crown is engraved in the centre of the breastplate with an emu to the right side, and a kangaroo to the left. Leaf sprigs are in both curves. This breastplate measures 150 mm (h) x 205 mm (w) x 20 mm (d).

This breastplate was awarded to Timothy, one of a group of Aboriginal men who rescued drowning merchant seamen off the coast of Batemans Bay, NSW, around 1840. The men formed a human chain to brave the surf and rescue the stranded crew of the wrecked schooner. The breastplates awarded to the men were commissioned by a naval captain who was unable to secure government funding to reward the men for their bravery. 

Breastplates are illustrative of Aboriginal-white relations during the early settlement period of Australia. The Governor of NSW, Lachlan Macquarie (1762-1824) presented breastplates to Aboriginal people in an attempt to combat the deteriorating relations between colonists and Indigenous people. Later it became common for others to present breastplates. By 1946, when the last known breastplate was presented, hundreds, if not thousands, had been awarded. They were presented for many reasons, such as rewards for heroic acts or faithful service, or as part of processes of negotiation and exchange.

Macquarie's strategy of presenting breastplates was an attempt to establish a system of 'chieftainship' whereby each Aboriginal 'tribe' had a chief who would settle internal matters and who would be the intermediary between his tribe and the government. This system was very different to the democratic systems favoured by Aboriginal people at the time, which were based around consensus decision making by a group of elders. The 'chiefs' were to be presented with a brass 'badge of distinction', or breastplate, engraved with their name and tribe, identifying them and their status. 

Throughout their history, breastplates generally remained crescent-shaped. Not all featured decoration additional to the inscription, but there was considerable variety in the engraved designs of decorated plates. Kangaroos and emus with their heads turned looking over their shoulders are common designs. Other Australian animals found on breastplates include platypuses, lyrebirds, lizards and snakes. Grass and grass trees are the most common plants to be found. Other common motifs include Aboriginal people, sprigs, weapons and coronets.

records.title: Aboriginal breastplate for Paddy, King of Nive Downs and Duke of Tambo
places: Nive Downs, Augathella, Queensland, Australia (Associated place)
Tambo, Queensland, Australia (Associated place)
records.collection: Paddy King of Nive Downs and Duke of Tambo collection
records.physical_description: A crescentric shaped brass breastplate with the inscription 'PADDY / King of Nive Downs / and / Duke of Tambo'. The breastplate has a hole at the edge of each horn and a metal link neck chain has been threaded through the holes.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a crescentric brass breastplate with the inscription 'PADDY / King of Nive Downs, / and / Duke of Tambo.' Charles Boydell Dutton, Archibald Francis Dutton and William George Bell were amongst the first to apply for leases in the Mitchell District, which would become the sheep stations Nive Downs and Tambo Station. The Duttons sold Nive Downs in 1866 and the Dutton and Bell families both resided at Tambo Station. The stations were on the land of the Dharawala people and so it is possible that Paddy was a Dharawala man. 

The close relationship between the two properties suggests the possibility that the breastplate was given to Paddy by the Duttons prior to 1866. However, if the plate was presented after the Duttons sold Nive Downs, the wording could reflect the relationship between the station and the closest town. Breastplates are a tangible record of relationships between individual settlers and Aboriginal people around mainland Australia. They were frequently presented to recognise the 'Chief' or 'King' of a 'tribe', which was often an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. They also often recognise service, such as on a pastoral property. The National Museum holds the largest collection of breastplates in the world, most of which are the only known record of the life of the recipient. This is the only breastplate in the collection to use both 'king' and 'duke' in the title.

records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of 17 objects worn or used by Bruce Breaden in his daily work as head stockman on cattle stations in central Australia: an Akubra hat, a pair of R. M. Williams elastic-sided boots, a pair of R. M. Williams trousers, two long-sleeved shirts, a long-sleeved jumper, a synthetic belt (featuring a leather pocket knife pouch or sheath, counted as a separate object), a pocket knife, a Syd Hill Giltrow Poley saddle (with breastplate, stirrups, girth and surcingle attached), a leather quartpot holder, a leather saddlebag, a bridle, a pair of reins, a plaited fibre lead rope, a hobble chain and a branding iron. 

A Luritja man born at Tempe Downs, where he also first started work, Bruce Breaden fought for 25 years until he secured land rights over the Tempe Downs/Middleton Ponds region on behalf of his people. Breaden's stockman's kit represents the history of Aboriginal people in the cattle industry of northern Australia and their essential contribution to the development of what is now one of the nation's major exports (and a major source of national iconography). The collection also represents Breaden's personal expertise in traditional skills so vital to the industry before the advent of aerial mustering, beef roads and satellite technology.

records.title: Aboriginal wooden container
records.physical_description: An oval shaped curved wooden vessel. Both the inside and outside are red in colour. There are layers of wood coming apart on the outside edge.
records.significance_statement:
The collection comprises a broad range of objects including batiks, pokerwork carvings, paintings and pastel drawings on paper and other art and craft items, bibles and school readers in Pitjantjatjara, drawings by school children, photograph albums, videos and a small number of stone implements.

The collection is significant for the depth and range of material associated with a single Aboriginal settlement at Ernabella, now known as Pukatja, its art centre and with Deaconness Winifred Hilliard who was the Arts Advisor to Ernabella between 1954 and 1986. The collection largely dates to this period. Along with other material previously donated by Hilliard, this collection documents the history of Ernabella and the women's art movement there between, but not limited to, 1954 and 1986.

records.physical_description: A crescentric, slighly convex brass breastplate without chain, obverse engraved 'TOMMY / KING OF / CONNAI',  with an emu on the left and a kangaroo on the right.There are three holes to fit a neck chain, of which two appear broken off.
records.significance_statement:
This collection is comprised of seventeen Australian Indigenous breastplates (also known as king plates or gorgets). They come from a collection accumulated by L. Richard Smith, a noted collector of medals and porcelain. The breastplates are associated with Indigenous people from Queensland, New South Wales and Western Australia.  The breastplates are all metal, of varying size, and are generally crescent shaped. Each is inscribed with the recipient's name, and many include an associated region and an honorary title such as 'king', 'queen' or 'chief'.  

During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, government authorities and settlers gave breastplates to Indigenous people for a variety of reasons. They were used as a way of selecting and identifying local elders to act as intermediaries between settlers and local Indigenous people. They were also given out in recognition of service and/or assistance (for example to Aboriginal stockmen or for saving people from ship wrecks).  As such, they are significant cross-cultural objects that document early interaction between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in different regions of Australia.  They often record the names of Indigenous people, and the station or region with which they are associated; people who are not otherwise represented in historical records. The collection is also significant in expanding the geographical scope of the National Museum's existing breastplate collection.

records.description: Anne Ranse is a nurse and midwife whose first two jobs were nursing at Coober Pedy in outback South Australia, from 1969, and at Ernabella, an Aboriginal town in the north-west of the same state, between 1972 and 1977. Currently, she is a deacon with the Anglican Church in Canberra. At Ernabella, where most of this collection originated, Ranse developed close relationships with many of the Aboriginal women living in the area and many of the items in her collection were gifts from them.
records.physical_description: A limited edition pamphlet with a brown card cover in landscape orientation. The maroon and red printed title along the right panel of the cover page reads, 'CENTRAL / AUSTRALIAN / ABORIGINAL / PAINTINGS / BRILLIANT ABSTRACT / DESIGNS OF THE / PITJANTJATJARA'. The pamphlet consists of introductory notes and seven coloured plates or prints in red, brown and navy-blue, with some black printed text underneath each of them. The plates or prints are interweaved with a tissue paper. The pamphlet contains 16 unnumbered pages.
records.significance_statement:
The Anne Ranse collection comprises art and craft items, including batik fabrics, pokerwork sculptures and the less common stone animal carvings, and a few weapons from Ernabella as well as a small number of Aboriginal stone implements, correspondence and personal items.

Anne Ranse is a nurse by training who worked at Ernabella, in north-western South Australia, between 1972 and 1977. She developed close relationships with Aboriginal women there and they gave many of the items in this collection to Ranse. The art and craft items are also important as examples of works produced at Ernabella over a relatively short period. Ranse’s copy of "Handbook of Medical Treatment" is symbolic of her work as a nurse in remote places like Ernabella and Coober Pedy where she had worked earlier. The correspondence relates to important people associated with Ernabella - Charles Duguid, Winifred Hilliard and Purki Edwards.

Donated by Archdeacon Anne Ranse

records.title: Michael Kinsela, Chief of Cudgelbong
records.collection: Michael Kinsela, Chief of Cudgelbong Breastplate collection
records.physical_description: A pale gold-brown metal breastplate with the inscription, 'MICHAEL KINSELA / CHIEF of CUDGELBONG', engraved into the surface below an image of a male figure depicted wearing a breastplate around his neck and knee length breeches. In his right hand he holds a brace of fish, while a pronged spear with an impaled fish is held in his left. A stylised image of a kangaroo appears on the upper right hand side and an emu on the upper left. Holes have been punched into the two horns of the breastplate, each threaded with an oval metal link. The back is dark brown with an uneven surface.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a brass breastplate presented around 1840 to Michael Kinsela of Cudgelbong, a Kamberri man. It was given to (or collected by) pastoralist George Sibley, who owned the original 'Red Hill' property at Gundaroo, New South Wales, in the 1850s and whose descendants still live in the region today. Since 'Cudgelbong' is probably a variation of 'cudgegong', an Aboriginal word meaning 'red hill', it is highly likely that the land around Gundaroo was Michael Kinsela's country.

By the 1830s it was common practice to present Aboriginal people perceived as local leaders with breastplates in an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. Breastplates were also presented as a reward for labour or particular acts of heroism. It is possible Michael Kinsela worked as a tracker for the police and took his non-indigenous name from Patrick Kinsela, who was appointed to the position of Chief Constable of Queanbeyan in February 1838. Some of the descendants of Patrick Kinsela have, like the Sibleys, remained in the region. Thus Michael Kinsela's breastplate is not only tangible evidence of a named individual - a rare record for an Aboriginal person in colonial Australian history - but is unusual for having a relatively strong provenance to two families and locations with an ongoing local history.

records.significance_statement:
The collection is comprised of 35 objects including prints, photographs, woven materials, a cricket trophy and other items. The ATSIAA 2 collection is an adjunct to the original, much larger Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection, (ATSIAA), collected between 1967 and 2005 by employees of a number of Indigenous government bodies.  The larger collection is comprised of 2313 objects.  The material in the current collection did not appear on the original inventory and was not stored with the original items. The objects were located in a storeroom within the Department of Families, Housing, Community Services and Indigenous Affairs in 2010.  It is however, indisputably linked to the original ATSIAA collection.  All the items are in good or reasonable condition.

The collection is significant as it complements the original collection and fills geographical and stylistic gaps in the NMA's collection of cultural material relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. It also includes some provenanced objects that may prove useful in documenting some of the existing ATSIAA material.  The accrual of these two collections has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.  The collections span the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved.  As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the ATSIAA collection 2 is also significant, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Four Aboriginal Legal Service posters
records.physical_description: Four Aboriginal Legal Service posters.  Each is a white rectangular poster with black, red and yellow print and drawings. Text across the top of each poster reads "ABORIGINAL LEGAL SERVICE". There are three drawings beneath the title.  Below the drawings is text in black print that reads "When in trouble & need help and advice: 'DON'T COP IT SWEET'''. Further details of contact places and telephone numbers are listed at the bottom of each poster.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a range of items associated with Winifred Hilliard and the Ernabella Aboriginal community in Central Australia. It includes art and craft items, film equipment, a camera and other items used by Hilliard in her work as an arts advisor with Aboriginal people at Ernabella, as well as her photograph albums, awards and items relating to her involvement in the Presbyterian and later Uniting Church. Collectively, it is representative of Hilliard's adult life, particularly at Ernabella.

Winifred Hilliard was a Presbyterian and later Uniting Church deaconess who, from 1954 until her retirement in 1986, worked as arts advisor in the Ernabella art centre. Hilliard and her work with the community contributed  to the development of the Aboriginal arts and craft industry in central Australia. Established in 1948, Ernabella Arts is one of the longest continually running Aboriginal art centres in Australia and is noted for the range of items produced there. It was at Ernabella that the first batiks were produced by Aboriginal artists in the early 1970s, with artists from Ernabella teaching the technique to Indigenous artists in other communities. Hilliard was influential in introducing new art forms at Ernabella and it was Hilliard who suggested Ernabella artists try batik. This brought them national and international recognition from the 1970s for several decades. This collection highlights the contribution of Hilliard and the artists in making Ernabella a key organisation in the development of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art industry.

records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises protest material relating to the South African Liberation centre, a site of anti-apartheid protest in Canberra, from late1985 to the early 1990s. The collection includes photographs, banners, placards and posters and is significant in terms of Australia's place in the anti-apartheid movement. Although Australia has never broken diplomatic relations with South Africa it is clear that many Australians found South African apartheid unacceptable and were prepared to go to great lengths to articulate their objection to its continued existence.

The nature of protest in Australia has changed in the 1980s and 1990s. The anti-apartheid campaigns demonstrate the Australian Federal F's changing interpretation of police powers in relation to the acts governing unlawful assembly, summary offences, disorderly conduct, public nuisance and similar legislation invoked when dealing with public protest.

records.description: Lorne station is approximately 46km south of Blackall on the Adavale road and Bonnie Doon station is about another 25 km south from Lorne also on the Adavale Rd.

records.significance_statement:
This collection is comprised of seventeen Australian Indigenous breastplates (also known as king plates or gorgets). They come from a collection accumulated by L. Richard Smith, a noted collector of medals and porcelain. The breastplates are associated with Indigenous people from Queensland, New South Wales and Western Australia.  The breastplates are all metal, of varying size, and are generally crescent shaped. Each is inscribed with the recipient's name, and many include an associated region and an honorary title such as 'king', 'queen' or 'chief'.  

During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, government authorities and settlers gave breastplates to Indigenous people for a variety of reasons. They were used as a way of selecting and identifying local elders to act as intermediaries between settlers and local Indigenous people. They were also given out in recognition of service and/or assistance (for example to Aboriginal stockmen or for saving people from ship wrecks).  As such, they are significant cross-cultural objects that document early interaction between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in different regions of Australia.  They often record the names of Indigenous people, and the station or region with which they are associated; people who are not otherwise represented in historical records. The collection is also significant in expanding the geographical scope of the National Museum's existing breastplate collection.

records.description: Edmund Milne (1861-1917) was born in England and emigrated to Queensland with his parents 19 months later. He had had personal contact with Aboriginal people throughout his life, from when he was a small boy in Queensland and, from the late 1860s, in New South Wales. This contact may have led him to recording the names of Aboriginal people associated with particular objects in his collection, at a time when this was rarely done. Milne seems to have begun actively collecting Indigenous artefacts in the early 1880s and was still acquiring objects a few months before his death in 1917. His work with the NSW Railways (1876-1917) enabled him to meet a broad range of people who facilitated his collecting and associated activities like visiting Aboriginal sites. From at least the time he lived at Orange NSW (1906-1915), and later at Ryde (1915-1917), near to Sydney city, he displayed his collection at his home. In addition to a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts, Milne's collection included artefacts from the South Pacific and prehistoric implements from Egypt, France and England. In his will dated 12 December 1916, Milne bequeathed his “Anthropological collection” to the “first Federal Museum opened in the Federal Capital”. The collection remained at Ryde until early 1931 when it was acquired by the Australian Institute of Anatomy in Canberra. It remained there until the Institute's collections were transferred to the National Museum of Australia in 1985.
records.physical_description: A crescentric brass breastplate with a hole at the edge of each horn to attach a chain. Engraved on the anterior surface is "NEDDY / KING OF NEIS VALLEY".  A sun symbol is engraved on the plate's centre.

records.title: Aboriginal Provisional Government
records.physical_description: Black t-shirt, size 10. Front has map of Australia printed with Aboriginal flag colours as landmass. Sun in centre has 'ABORIGINAL PROVISIONAL GOVERNMENT' printed on it. Back, white lettering with 'OUR GOVERNMENT OUR LAND'
records.significance_statement:
The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre collection no 2 consists of three t-shirts. The first, a black t-shirt, has a map of Australia in black, yellow and red. The words “ABORIGINAL PROVISIONAL GOVERNMENT” and “OUR GOVERNMENT OUR LAND” are printed on the front and back respectively. The second t-shirt is blue background with a coastal map of northern Tasmania in black, yellow and red, with the words “ROCKY CAPE” and RECLAIMED 1991” printed above and below the map. An Aboriginal flag and 'LAND IS LIFE' are printed on the back.  The third t-shirt is white. The wording printed above and below the red, yellow and black Tasmanian emblem reads, “TASMANIAN ABORIGINES CELEBRATE 8 "YEARS OF REOCCUPATION OF OYSTER COVE 1984-1992". A chain with the words, "FROM OPPRESSION TO REPOSSESSION" is printed on the back.
  
This collection was purchased from the Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC), Hobart in 1992. The 
t-shirts were produced by the TAC for sale at various cultural festivals, such as the Rocky Cape festival, which were held each year to enable Tasmanian Aboriginal people to return to and to reclaim ownership of their traditional lands.  Oyster Cove is significant as the place where Aboriginal people from Wybelana (Flinders Island) were sent by Chief Protector of Aborigines for Port Phillip (Victoria), George Augustus Robinson, in the 1800s to "save the last remaining Aboriginals".   Formerly the Tasmanian Aboriginal Information Service, the TAC was established in 1973 and commenced to petition the Tasmanian Parliament in 1977 with what became known as the Aboriginal Land Claim.  The t-shirts in this collection are associated with the land claim petition and were purchased in 1990 for inclusion in the NHC.  The timing of their purchase, reflected in the wording of the first  t-shirt, also coincided with the establishment of the Aboriginal Provisional Government, an organisation which seeks sovereignty, land rights and self-determination for all Aboriginal Australians.  In 1995, following years of lobbying by the Aboriginal community, the Tasmanian government passed the Aboriginal Lands Act, which acknowledged the dispossession of, and sought reconciliation with, Tasmanian Aboriginal People, by returning twelve parcels of land of 'historic and cultural significance'.  The Act provided for an elected Aboriginal Land Council to own and sustainably manage these lands. Aboriginal activist Michael Mansell later pointed out that the land returned comprised under 0.001 percent of Tasmania.

places: Vanrook, Queensland, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped, brass breastplate with a hole at the apex of each of the two horns, where a chain is attached. The anterior surface features engraved text which reads 'TOBY / KING OF VANROOK', and an engraved curvilinear motif at the centre. Within the engraved lettering and motif are the remnants of red, black and green materials. A copper coloured spot is visible above the letter K in 'KING'. The attached chain has a dark brass patina, and one end of the chain has a ferrous based metal, parrot style clasp which is corroded. The reverse of the breastplate features a rectangular, white paper adhesive label with the numbers '6342' handwritten in ink, and the remnants of a circular label.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a crescent-shaped brass breastplate with a chain attached to each end.  The plate is inscribed 'TOBY / KING OF VANROOK' and bears traces of a red and black enamel-like substance that once filled in the lettering. It is unknown who presented it to 'Toby' or when. The location 'Vanrook' is Vanrook Station in the region of the Gulf of Carpentaria, north Queensland, about 120 kilometres north-east of Normanton.  It is located on the border between the lands of the Kurtjar and Kunjen people, inland from Delta Downs station.

As with many of the Aboriginal people named on breastplates, there is no other known record of 'Toby'.  It is likely that he was a Kunjen or Kurtjar man who worked at Vanrook. Breastplates are a tangible record of relationships between individual settlers and Aboriginal people around mainland Australia. They were frequently presented to recognise the 'Chief' or 'King' of a 'tribe', in attempt to aid peaceable settlement. They also often recognise service, such as on a pastoral property. The National Museum holds the largest collection of breastplates in the world, most of which are the only known record of the life of the recipient.

records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of 17 objects worn or used by Bruce Breaden in his daily work as head stockman on cattle stations in central Australia: an Akubra hat, a pair of R. M. Williams elastic-sided boots, a pair of R. M. Williams trousers, two long-sleeved shirts, a long-sleeved jumper, a synthetic belt (featuring a leather pocket knife pouch or sheath, counted as a separate object), a pocket knife, a Syd Hill Giltrow Poley saddle (with breastplate, stirrups, girth and surcingle attached), a leather quartpot holder, a leather saddlebag, a bridle, a pair of reins, a plaited fibre lead rope, a hobble chain and a branding iron. 

A Luritja man born at Tempe Downs, where he also first started work, Bruce Breaden fought for 25 years until he secured land rights over the Tempe Downs/Middleton Ponds region on behalf of his people. Breaden's stockman's kit represents the history of Aboriginal people in the cattle industry of northern Australia and their essential contribution to the development of what is now one of the nation's major exports (and a major source of national iconography). The collection also represents Breaden's personal expertise in traditional skills so vital to the industry before the advent of aerial mustering, beef roads and satellite technology.

records.title: Land rights poster: 'YOU ARE ON ABORIGINAL LAND'
records.physical_description: Portrait format poster on paper, with a central figure of an Aboriginal woman dressed in a green t-shirt and patterned skirt standing on yellow coloured ground with stylised grass and the sea behind her. She is bordered on left and right sides with thin vertical lines in red, yellow and black. The words 'YOU ARE ON ABORIGINAL LAND' is printed below the image with production details printed on yellow vertical line on the left and at the bottom right of the margin. There is a small tear one third of the way down the poster on teh left hand side.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises four posters collected by Ali Kazak that represent concerns for Indigenous rights in Australia in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Kazak collected the posters during this time, and kept them in his possession until he offered them for donation to the Museum in late 2016. Three of the posters bear messages of protest regarding land rights, mining and dispossession. The fourth poster is a request for funding assistance for Australia's first Indigenous community school, the Black Community School in Townsville, which was established by Eddie Mabo in 1973. It, too, has an underlying message of protest against issues related to racism and rights for Indigenous peoples in Australia.

The poster designed by Marie McMahon is especially striking, showing a Tiwi woman standing on a beach with her hair blowing in the wind. McMahon was travelling with Tiwi man, Piparo (Winnie Munkara), on Bathurst Island in 1980 when they came across two businessmen on the island without permission. McMahon recalls how they came ''head-to-head on the narrow bush track and Winnie confronted the Darwin businessmen in theatrical Tiwi style, with dramatic stick waving and cracking on the ground and shouting “Tikilaru is not your country”. That event remained in my mind as a demonstration of land ownership from an Aboriginal perspective.’

records.significance_statement:
The collection, donated by the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation between 2000 and 2002, includes photographs, documents, banners, posters and cultural material - a total of 111 separately listed items.  The collection reflects the activity of the Council, the events of 'Corroboree 2000' and the corresponding, nation-wide series of festivals and walks.  Included are examples of the broad range of promotional and educational materials produced by the Council.  The objects are in good condition and reference material is available for identification and further research.

The Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation was established in 1991 following a unanimous decision by the Commonwealth Parliament to recognise the importance of reconciliation and to create a formal reconciliation process in the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation Act 1991.  A goal of increased awareness and achievement in the area of reconciliation by the year 2001 was set.  In that ten year period, the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation worked through a program of extensive community consultation.  At the end of its term, the Council produced several 'Documents for Reconciliation', including a strategy entitled Roadmap to Reconciliation.  These documents were launched as part of 'Corroboree 2000', at the Sydney Opera House on 27 May 2000.  An independent foundation, Reconciliation Australia, was established to continue the work of the Council following its closure and final submissions to the Commonwealth Government.

records.physical_description: A circular corroded metal badge which has a drawing of the Aboriginal Flag in the centre. The text 'ABORIGINAL' is printed above the flag and 'LAND RIGHTS' is printed beneath the flag.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.physical_description: A colour poster with a photograph of three children and a man carrying two kangaroos between them in the bush. There is printed Japanese writing above and below the photograph.
records.significance_statement:
The collection comprises a broad range of objects including batiks, pokerwork carvings, paintings and pastel drawings on paper and other art and craft items, bibles and school readers in Pitjantjatjara, drawings by school children, photograph albums, videos and a small number of stone implements.

The collection is significant for the depth and range of material associated with a single Aboriginal settlement at Ernabella, now known as Pukatja, its art centre and with Deaconness Winifred Hilliard who was the Arts Advisor to Ernabella between 1954 and 1986. The collection largely dates to this period. Along with other material previously donated by Hilliard, this collection documents the history of Ernabella and the women's art movement there between, but not limited to, 1954 and 1986.

records.significance_statement:
The collection comprises 18 Aboriginal artefacts, including spearthrowers, wooden dishes and stone tools, mainly acquired by filmmaker Ian Dunlop in the 1960s from the Western Desert in Western Australia, northern Queensland and the Northern Territory. The collection also includes Dunlop's briefcase and a Foundation for Aboriginal Affairs plastic bag.

The Aboriginal artefacts are significant for their high level of documentation. They largely comprise items made by people living in the 'desert' for their own use or that Dunlop filmed in the 1960s being made or used. The names of the people who made or used them are also often known. As a filmmaker who produced a number of important films on Aboriginal cultures from the 1960s to the 1990s, Dunlop is an important figure in the history of Australian ethnographic film production. He was involved with the Foundation for Aboriginal Affairs, an early Australian civil rights organisation.

Donated by Ian Dunlop

records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

The collection is significant for the depth and range of material associated with a single Aboriginal settlement at Ernabella, now known as Pukatja, its art centre and with Deaconness Winifred Hilliard who was the Arts Advisor to Ernabella between 1954 and 1986. records.physical_description: A circular, yellow, plastic coated metal badge with an illustration of a lizard in orange and brown. Beneath the lizard is text that reads 'ABORIGINAL VOTES COUNT'.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.physical_description: A certificate on paper for Bevon Hayward Pooaraar with text that reads 'THE MUSEUMS AND ART GALLERIES BOARD / OF THE NORTHERN TERRITORY / is pleased to present the 'Memorial Award / for Mawalan's Eldest Son / for the best artwork in the open media category to Bevon Hayward Pooaraar at the SEVENTH NATIONAL ABORIGINAL ART AWARD 1990 / … /'.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises three artist diaries  belonging to Pooaraar (Bevan Hayward), an 'urban' Noongar artist, born in southwest Western Australia, who provided an important body of art in the1980s and 1990s. An award certificate and a collection of personal papers and letters are held in the NMA Archive collection.

Friend Simon O'Mallon described Pooaraar (1939-2004) as a quiet man of few words. This collection allows a glimpse into Pooaraar's philosophy, the way he developed his work and his responses to issues affecting Indigenous peoples. It also has strong links to other artworks created by Pooaraar in the National Historical Collection.

Donated by Simon O'Mallon

records.title: Bracelet in Aboriginal colours
records.description: This bracelet was presented by Joy Williams to Peter Read in 1983. Together, they travelled to the Erambie Mission, Cowra to see Joy’s extended family. It is believed that they were made by Joy as a celebration of her regaining her Aboriginal identity and given to Read in appreciation for his work in Link-up.
records.physical_description: A bracelet of beads in black, red and yellow on a plastic string with a metal clasp. At the centre, there are three yellow beads, with two black beads on either side, and the remainder are red beds.
records.significance_statement:
The Joy Williams collection comprises a plaited wool hatband and plastic bead bracelet in Aboriginal colours, a framed Albert Namatjira print, two scrapbooks of 1980s newspaper cuttings concerning Indigenous matters and a manuscript of a collection of Joy Williams' poems entitled 'Wiradjuri Woman Valley Man Love'. The hatband, bracelet and manuscript are in good condition. The scrapbooks are fragile with loose pages and the print and frame are scratched and stained.

Joy Williams (1942-2006) was a significant member of those children removed under government and church policies directed at Aboriginal communities. Joy's mother and daughter were also removed as children, so that three generations of one family were affected by these policies. Because of her fair complexion Joy was one of those sent, not to Aboriginal children's homes, but to a 'white' orphanage. In the 1990s she unsuccessfully sued the state for failure of duty of care; one of the first people in that situation to do so. Joy was also an important member of the Link-Up organisation, being a committee member from 1983 until her death. She was also representative of those, who although reunited with their family, found the Link-Up community to be the one that was their most significant Aboriginal 'community'.

Donated by Professor Peter Read

The poem reads 'By old Mulwarree's banks I sit, / The last of all my race; / While swiftly sun-cloud shadows flit / Across my native place. ...'. Text along the bottom of the page reads 'Goulburn, July, 1901 / A.C. BARRETT.'.

records.title: Breastplate inscribed Queen Milly of the Burunji [Barunji] 1870
records.collection: Queen Milly of the Barunji Breastplate collection
records.description: The small stamped crown motif on the reverse of the breastplate suggests it was of government issue.
records.physical_description: A crescent-shaped, slightly convex brass breastplate with a hole at the apex of each of the two horns. The anterior surface features engraved zigzagged text which reads 'QUEEN MILLY / OF THE / BURUNJI[sic]', flanked by a line engraving of an emu to the left and kangaroo to the right, and the date 1870, with '18' at the upper left and '70' at the upper right. The edge is stamped with a decorative scalloped border. The reverse features stippling around the edge of the plate, and a small stamped crown motif at the centre. The holes in the horns of the crescent exhibit evidence of wear.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a brass breastplate presented in 1870 to Queen Milly, a Burunji (Parundji) woman from the Paroo River region in northwestern New South Wales.

By the 1830s it was common practice to present Aboriginal people perceived as local leaders with breastplates in an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. Breastplates were also presented as a reward for labour or particular acts of heroism. However, fewer than ten per cent of known breastplates were presented to women. In the absence of unequivocal provenance, the crown motif stamped on the reverse of Queen Milly's breastplate indicates that it was of government issue, suggesting that she - perhaps the wife of the King of the Burunji, although no such breastplate has yet been found - may have been chosen to help peacefully mediate settlement at a time of potentially volatile exchanges between her people and the pastoralists. She may have also assisted surveyors pegging out new runs, or been involved in the distribution of government rations at Aboriginal camps.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Walking Together - Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation badge
records.physical_description: A black metal circular badge with a plastic coating over a printed design featuring a black background and white text reading 'WALKING / TOGETHER' across the top, partially overlaying a yellow, red and green sun motif. There are stylised lines, dots and triangles in yellow, red and green extending diagonally from the sun to the bottom of the badge. Curved around the lower edge of the badge is white text reading 'COUNCIL FOR ABORIGINAL RECONCILIATION'. A metal safety pin is attached to the verso.
records.significance_statement:
The Deborah Turner collection is comprised of 103 badges - 69 of which reference the Communist Party of Australia's (CPA) involvement in a range of emancipatory projects: such as anti-war appeals, Australian Federal Politics, indigenous equality and woman's rights. The other 33 badges reference May Day, a celebration of the labour movement and the fight for an eight hour day. 

The badges in the Deborah Turner collection cover an extensive period in the history of the CPA and the South Coast District Committee (SCDC). The 69 disparate badges in the collection account for a number of the Communist Party interests in Australia over a fifty year period. The other 33 badges in the Deborah Turner collection relate to May Day. This collection speaks to the connection between protest paraphernalia and a political message, and will form a significant collection of political campaign badges from the mid 20th Century.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: King Nobby of Widgee Widgee
places: Widgee, Queensland, Australia (Associated place)
records.collection: King Nobby of Widgee Widgee collection
records.physical_description: A crescentric shaped brass breastplate with the inscription 'WIDGEE / KING NOBBY / WIDGEE'. On either side of this inscription are engravings of a kangaroo and an emu. The breastplate has a hole at the edge of each horn.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a crescentric brass breastplate with the inscription 'WIDGEE / KING NOBBY / WIDGEE' and a regardant kangaroo and emu. The breastplate was preserved by James John Goode Caulfield, who was the head stockman on Widgee Widgee Station, west of Gympie. 

Widgee Widgee was one of the first and largest pastoral properties to be established along the Mary River. Settled in 1849 the station was a site of conflict between settlers and the Gubbi Gubbi people throughout the 1850s and into the 1860s. It is unknown who 'Nobby' was, but it is likely that he was a Gubbi Gubbi man employed on the station as a stockman. Breastplates are a tangible record of relationships between individual settlers and Aboriginal people around mainland Australia. They were frequently presented to recognise the 'Chief' or 'King' of a 'tribe', which was often an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. They also often recognise service, such as on a pastoral property. The National Museum holds the largest collection of breastplates in the world, most of which are the only known record of the life of the recipient.

records.description: Edmund Milne (1861-1917) was born in England and emigrated to Queensland with his parents 19 months later. He had had personal contact with Aboriginal people throughout his life, from when he was a small boy in Queensland and, from the late 1860s, in New South Wales. This contact may have led him to recording the names of Aboriginal people associated with particular objects in his collection, at a time when this was rarely done. Milne seems to have begun actively collecting Indigenous artefacts in the early 1880s and was still acquiring objects a few months before his death in 1917. His work with the NSW Railways (1876-1917) enabled him to meet a broad range of people who facilitated his collecting and associated activities like visiting Aboriginal sites. From at least the time he lived at Orange NSW (1906-1915), and later at Ryde (1915-1917), near to Sydney city, he displayed his collection at his home. In addition to a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts, Milne's collection included artefacts from the South Pacific and prehistoric implements from Egypt, France and England. In his will dated 12 December 1916, Milne bequeathed his “Anthropological collection” to the “first Federal Museum opened in the Federal Capital”. The collection remained at Ryde until early 1931 when it was acquired by the Australian Institute of Anatomy in Canberra. It remained there until the Institute's collections were transferred to the National Museum of Australia in 1985.

records.significance_statement:
The Eileen Morgan collection comprises a replica bottle doll swathed in blue and white fabric, a replica lamp and implements (a stick and a hammerstone) used to construct the doll. 

Children on Aboriginal missions often had to make their own toys and devise games to play.This toy doll is a 'replica' of the same type of doll Eileen Morgan made as a child at Wallaga Lake Aboriginal Mission, on the south coast of NSW, during the 1930s. The lamp, also a replica, shows how people in at Wallaga Lake (and other) missions solved one of the problems of fringe dwelling, the provision of light in dwellings, by using putting a wick in a tin filled with animal fat.

records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Washing day, Aboriginal mission station. August, 1952
records.physical_description: A carbonite pencil drawing on plain artist's drawing paper. The drawing is of an Aboriginal woman washing clothes and a child sitting on a can.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of 101 sketches  drawn in 1952-53 by Noelle Sandwith, an English artist visiting Australia who was intent on drawing 'unusual subjects' and set her sights on the Australian outback.    A wide variety of groups and people within the Australian community are examined through the sketches.  These include Aboriginal people and their involvement in missions, life on the outskirts of town, incarceration and the role of the Protectorate.  Post-war immigration is represented through the involvement of Greeks and Italians running cafes in small country towns.  Community groups representing rural and outback people such as the Australian Inland Mission, Salvation Army, Country Women's Association and the Flying Doctor's Service also rate a significant mention.  Other issues and people who are explored include Afghan cameleers, social events such as rodeos and drinking, life in the shearing shed and the role of the local police to name a few.

On the recommendation of the Australian Inland Mission, Ms Sandwith set out for south-western Queensland and down the Birdsville track to Marree in South Australia.  She undertook this journey on her own, allowing her the freedom to travel where she wanted and to record the lives of people in the outback as she viewed it. Great changes occurred in Australia in the 1950s.  Society changed relatively quickly with the influx of immigrants following WWII.  Policies of assimilation were at their height and this extended to both the indigenous people of Australia and the newest groups of  immigrants.  This period of contact between the various sectors of the Australian community is one which of great interest to us today.  The sketches provide a view of outback society at this time and chronicle the relationships between various groups and people. There was great interest in the treatment of Australia's Indigenous inhabitants during this period.  The sketches provide a personal view of the perceptions of European people towards Aboriginal people.  Several of the sketches slip into caricature when dealing with Aboriginal people and this also provides us with Sandwith's view.  Several poignant comments are made regarding the lifestyle and expectations of Aboriginal people.  Whilst these seem dated now, they are powerful reminders of the attitudes which prevailed at the time of sketching.

records.significance_statement:
This collection is comprised of seventeen Australian Indigenous breastplates (also known as king plates or gorgets). They come from a collection accumulated by L. Richard Smith, a noted collector of medals and porcelain. The breastplates are associated with Indigenous people from Queensland, New South Wales and Western Australia.  The breastplates are all metal, of varying size, and are generally crescent shaped. Each is inscribed with the recipient's name, and many include an associated region and an honorary title such as 'king', 'queen' or 'chief'.  

During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, government authorities and settlers gave breastplates to Indigenous people for a variety of reasons. They were used as a way of selecting and identifying local elders to act as intermediaries between settlers and local Indigenous people. They were also given out in recognition of service and/or assistance (for example to Aboriginal stockmen or for saving people from ship wrecks).  As such, they are significant cross-cultural objects that document early interaction between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in different regions of Australia.  They often record the names of Indigenous people, and the station or region with which they are associated; people who are not otherwise represented in historical records. The collection is also significant in expanding the geographical scope of the National Museum's existing breastplate collection.

The words 'SUPPORT PROVIDE INSPIRE' are below the mans hands and have a black, yellow and red background. records.significance_statement:
The collection is comprised of 35 objects including prints, photographs, woven materials, a cricket trophy and other items. The ATSIAA 2 collection is an adjunct to the original, much larger Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection, (ATSIAA), collected between 1967 and 2005 by employees of a number of Indigenous government bodies.  The larger collection is comprised of 2313 objects.  The material in the current collection did not appear on the original inventory and was not stored with the original items. The objects were located in a storeroom within the Department of Families, Housing, Community Services and Indigenous Affairs in 2010.  It is however, indisputably linked to the original ATSIAA collection.  All the items are in good or reasonable condition.

The collection is significant as it complements the original collection and fills geographical and stylistic gaps in the NMA's collection of cultural material relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. It also includes some provenanced objects that may prove useful in documenting some of the existing ATSIAA material.  The accrual of these two collections has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.  The collections span the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved.  As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the ATSIAA collection 2 is also significant, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Tasmanian Aboriginal model bark canoe by Rex Greeno
records.physical_description: A model canoe that is made up of three bundles of cut and rolled paperbark, which are bound together to form an elongated canoe-shaped vessel.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises of a model Tasmanian bark canoe made by Rex Greeno. The canoe is made up of three bark hulls consisting of many smaller bundles of cut and rolled paperbark which are bound together to form the distinctive canoe-shaped vessel.

Rex Greeno was born on Flinders Island in Bass Strait. His Aboriginal heritage comes from his mother, Dulcie Greeno, a noted shell necklace maker and his grandfather Silas Mansell who taught him mutton-birding, kangaroo and wallaby snaring, and making craypots and boats. A fisherman like his father, Greeno was inspired to make traditional Tasmanian paperbark canoes, after researching late eighteenth and early nineteenth century accounts by maritime explorers and other early European settlers to the island. Greeno created a number of full-scale bark canoes, one of which is in the Museum's National Historical Collection. He employed the same method of construction for ten model canoes created in 2012 for the 2013 Ten Days on the Island festival, held biennially in Tasmania. Paperbark canoes have not been seen in Tasmania since the early nineteenth century. A few model canoes from the nineteenth century made by Aboriginal people, survive in museum collections.

records.title: Aboriginal stockman belt and knife pouch
records.physical_description: A black leather-look belt with a silver coloured buckle, and a brown knife pouch threaded on it. The initials "TBB" have been scratched into the surface of the belt and the pouch. The brown knife pouch has a metal stud closure and is sewn together with yellow thread.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of 17 objects worn or used by Bruce Breaden in his daily work as head stockman on cattle stations in central Australia: an Akubra hat, a pair of R. M. Williams elastic-sided boots, a pair of R. M. Williams trousers, two long-sleeved shirts, a long-sleeved jumper, a synthetic belt (featuring a leather pocket knife pouch or sheath, counted as a separate object), a pocket knife, a Syd Hill Giltrow Poley saddle (with breastplate, stirrups, girth and surcingle attached), a leather quartpot holder, a leather saddlebag, a bridle, a pair of reins, a plaited fibre lead rope, a hobble chain and a branding iron. 

A Luritja man born at Tempe Downs, where he also first started work, Bruce Breaden fought for 25 years until he secured land rights over the Tempe Downs/Middleton Ponds region on behalf of his people. Breaden's stockman's kit represents the history of Aboriginal people in the cattle industry of northern Australia and their essential contribution to the development of what is now one of the nation's major exports (and a major source of national iconography). The collection also represents Breaden's personal expertise in traditional skills so vital to the industry before the advent of aerial mustering, beef roads and satellite technology.

records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a female Salvation Army uniform, with jacket, blouse, skirt, shoes and hat, along with a timbrel and Australian Christian stickers and T-shirts.  The fourteen items belonged to Cath Solomon, a member of the Salvation Army for more than 40 years.  The uniform is a winter variety and the stickers relate to the annual 'Praise Corroboree' at Parliament House, Canberra.  All items are in good condition and were supplied with relevant information.

The Salvation Army has been active in Australia since the early 1880s.  It has made a significant charitable contribution to Australian society and has become a recognisable organisation through its Red Shield Appeal, emergency housing programs, counselling services and 'Salvos Stores'.  Cath Solomon worked in Indigenous communities and children's ministry, becoming a Divisional Envoy in the Lakes Entrance and Bairnsdale areas.  The Salvation Army supports the process of reconciliation in Australia, having developed an Aboriginal Ministry Advisory Council (SAAMAC) in 1995 and the Multicultural and Indigenous Australia Council (SAMIAC) in 2004 to guide its efforts.

records.title: Scrapbook containing newspaper clippings relating to Woomera Aboriginal Corporation, March 88
records.description:
This scrapbook contains newspaper articles collected by Joy Williams. The newspaper articles date from the 1980s and 1990s and include stories about deaths in custody, land rights and protests by and against Aboriginal communities. They express Joy’s passionate interest in Aboriginal matters and trace her journey to becoming a highly respected Aboriginal elder and a committed and longstanding member of the Link-Up committee

Joy gave the scrapbook to Peter Read in 2003 when he agreed to write her biography
records.physical_description: A blue cardboard covered A3 sized scrapbook. The scrapbook cover features a pair of scissors and multiple colour images. Along the left side of the front cover is the handwritten text 'MARCH 88'. The scrapbook contains newspaper clippings. Between the cover and first page are multiple loose newspaper clippings and a yellow brochure, titled, 'WOOMERA / ABORIGINAL / CORPORATION'.
records.significance_statement:
The Joy Williams collection comprises a plaited wool hatband and plastic bead bracelet in Aboriginal colours, a framed Albert Namatjira print, two scrapbooks of 1980s newspaper cuttings concerning Indigenous matters and a manuscript of a collection of Joy Williams' poems entitled 'Wiradjuri Woman Valley Man Love'. The hatband, bracelet and manuscript are in good condition. The scrapbooks are fragile with loose pages and the print and frame are scratched and stained.

Joy Williams (1942-2006) was a significant member of those children removed under government and church policies directed at Aboriginal communities. Joy's mother and daughter were also removed as children, so that three generations of one family were affected by these policies. Because of her fair complexion Joy was one of those sent, not to Aboriginal children's homes, but to a 'white' orphanage. In the 1990s she unsuccessfully sued the state for failure of duty of care; one of the first people in that situation to do so. Joy was also an important member of the Link-Up organisation, being a committee member from 1983 until her death. She was also representative of those, who although reunited with their family, found the Link-Up community to be the one that was their most significant Aboriginal 'community'.

Donated by Professor Peter Read

records.title: The Stolen Generations: the removal of Aboriginal children in NSW 1883 to 1969
records.physical_description: A peach-coloured booklet with brown and white photograph of a group of Aboriginal children and a white carer on the front cover and wrapped around to the back. Cover title reads 'N.S.W. Ministry of Aboriginal Affairs / THE STOLEN / GENERATIONS / The Removal of Aboriginal Children / In NSW 1883 to 1969 / by Peter Read'.The inside printed title page reads '(New South Wales) Ministry of Aboriginal Affairs: / OCCASIONAL PAPER (No.1) / The Stolen Generations: the Removal of Aboriginal /Children in New South Wales 1883 to 1969 / by Peter Read (A.N.U.) / This paper was prepared for the Aboriginal Children's Research / Project (New South Wales Family and Children's Services Agency) and is published through their kind permission' Inscribed in ink on the title page 'Peter Read presented 'The Stolen Generations' / to the National Museum of Australia on / the day in which the Prime Minister made / his apology to the Stolen Generations / 13 February 2008 / Peter Read'.  It is an A5 size booklet with 21 pages of text and black and white illustrations.
records.significance_statement:
The collection compirses the booklet 'The Stolen Generations; the Removal of Aboriginal Children in NSW 1883 to 1969'  written by Read and printed by the NSW Ministry of Aboriginal Affairs, a black metallic badge in the shape of Australia with 'Sorry' inscribed on it, the card that the badge was originally pinned to, and a laminated pass  'Link-Up NSW Aboriginal Corporation Peter Read Public Officer'. All the items are in good condition. 

The work of the historian Peter Read (b 1945) was a crucial element in the understanding of the nation-wide practice of the removal of children of mixed descent from Aboriginal families and communities.  It was he who connected stated government policies with the hundreds of instances of removal of children from NSW communities. Further research found the same processes at work in all states and territories. Stated government policies and formal and informal policies of other institutions such as churches aimed to remove children of mixed descent from their communities and to raise them as 'whites'. The intention was that they assimilate fully into the 'white' community and not return to their Indigenous one. This process has had an enormous effect on the Indigenous community, creating both social disruption and personal grief. The title of this booklet is the first usage of the term 'stolen generations' - a term used in Prime Minister Rudd's Apology speech in February 2008.
