records.title: Aboriginal woven basket, Bendigo Victoria region
places: Bendigo, Victoria, Australia (Associated place)
records.description: Thought to have been made by Aboriginal people in the Huntly region (near Bendigo)and traded for food with a European family.. Four generations of that family have kept it ever since and used it as a sewing basket.
records.physical_description: An oval shaped undyed grass coiled basket with lid. White cotton has been threaded around the top coil of the basket and edge coil of the lid. The sides of the basket are buckled.
records.significance_statement:
The Sarah Watts collection consists of a small coil-woven rush basket of Indigenous origin that was traded to Sarah Watts for food around the Huntly region, north of Bendigo, in about 1880. The basket has been meticulously cared for and handed down through four generations of women. It was offered to the Museum for sale by Ms Carol Flint, the great-granddaughter of Sarah Watts.

The weaving of plant fibre into nets and baskets was an important and widespread tradition amongst Indigenous populations. Baskets were crucial in transporting food and other personal items, but with the invasion of their lands by European settlers, traditional Indigenous gathering practices were disrupted and baskets were increasingly used to trade for food and money. The basket in the Sarah Watts collection was made using the coil technique that was common to Indigenous populations living along the Murray and Yarra Rivers of Victoria, but its style suggests it was constructed specifically for a non-Indigenous market. It thus provides an insight into some of the ways in which Indigenous people responded to European dispossession, as well some of the ways in which Indigenous and non-Indigenous people interacted.

places: Lockhart River, Queensland, Australia (Place made)
records.description: "We love our culture.  These are the animals we eat." - Brenton Ludwick, 2002
records.physical_description: A linocut print in black ink on white paper depicting the Aboriginal flag with a dugong above and turtle below. The word Aboriginal is printed in reverse on the flag. Handwritten text in pencil below the print reads 'Aboriginal Flag Brenton'. The linocut is mounted under black matt-board.
records.significance_statement:
The Lockhart River State School Collection contains 67 prints made by children in years four to seven in 2002. The 51 lino prints and 16 monoprints capture a sense of life in Lockhart River from the children's perspective, particularly the beach and its importance to fishing and hunting.  Some subjects are familiar to children around Australia, such as pets, ice-cream, sporting teams and holidays.  Others are more specific to Lockhart River. The fauna of the area receives particular attention, with cassowaries, kangaroos, dugongs, black cockatoos, crocodiles, ants, snake eggs, turtles, eels and jellyfish all appearing. 

The prints were made as a part of the collaboration between the school and the Lockhart River Arts and Cultural Centre. The children took art classes at the Centre and worked with members of the Lockhart River Art Gang. The Cultural Centre was established in order to revitalise the communication of traditional Aboriginal culture of the region and create vocational opportunities for young people. The members of the Art Gang were the first generation of successful artists to emerge from Lockhart River, in the late 1990s, and the project with the school was an opportunity to introduce the next generation to their work and the potential of art as a vocation.

records.title: Signed Qantas Aboriginal cricket tour poster, 1988
records.collection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art (ATSIAA) collection no. 2

records.significance_statement:
The collection is comprised of 35 objects including prints, photographs, woven materials, a cricket trophy and other items. The ATSIAA 2 collection is an adjunct to the original, much larger Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection, (ATSIAA), collected between 1967 and 2005 by employees of a number of Indigenous government bodies.  The larger collection is comprised of 2313 objects.  The material in the current collection did not appear on the original inventory and was not stored with the original items. The objects were located in a storeroom within the Department of Families, Housing, Community Services and Indigenous Affairs in 2010.  It is however, indisputably linked to the original ATSIAA collection.  All the items are in good or reasonable condition.

The collection is significant as it complements the original collection and fills geographical and stylistic gaps in the NMA's collection of cultural material relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. It also includes some provenanced objects that may prove useful in documenting some of the existing ATSIAA material.  The accrual of these two collections has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.  The collections span the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved.  As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the ATSIAA collection 2 is also significant, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Folder containing material related to Australian schools involvement in projects connected to Aboriginal Reconciliation Council
records.physical_description: A folder containing material related to Australian schools involvement in projects connected to Aboriginal Reconciliation Council
records.significance_statement:
The collection, donated by the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation between 2000 and 2002, includes photographs, documents, banners, posters and cultural material - a total of 111 separately listed items.  The collection reflects the activity of the Council, the events of 'Corroboree 2000' and the corresponding, nation-wide series of festivals and walks.  Included are examples of the broad range of promotional and educational materials produced by the Council.  The objects are in good condition and reference material is available for identification and further research.

The Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation was established in 1991 following a unanimous decision by the Commonwealth Parliament to recognise the importance of reconciliation and to create a formal reconciliation process in the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation Act 1991.  A goal of increased awareness and achievement in the area of reconciliation by the year 2001 was set.  In that ten year period, the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation worked through a program of extensive community consultation.  At the end of its term, the Council produced several 'Documents for Reconciliation', including a strategy entitled Roadmap to Reconciliation.  These documents were launched as part of 'Corroboree 2000', at the Sydney Opera House on 27 May 2000.  An independent foundation, Reconciliation Australia, was established to continue the work of the Council following its closure and final submissions to the Commonwealth Government.

records.title: King Mulga of Coongie Lakes breastplate, 1911
places: Coongie Lake, South Australia, Australia (Associated place)
records.collection: King Mulga of Coongie Lakes Breastplate collection
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped brass breastplate engraved with the words 'KING MULGA / of / COONGIE LAKES / 1911'. It features engravings of a kangaroo, emu and Australian native trees. Three circular markings are impressed in the back of the breastplate in a vertical grouping. They include a government ordinance broad arrow, the letters 'WBW' superimposed over a crown, and the letters 'SA'. A chain is attached through two holes on either side.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a bronze breastplate presented in 1911 to King Mulga, a Yawarrawarrka man living in the Coongie Lakes region northwest of Innamincka, South Australia.

By the 1830s it was common practice to present Aboriginal people perceived as local leaders with breastplates in an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. Breastplates were also presented as a reward for labour or particular acts of heroism. The exact provenance of King Mulga's breastplate is currently unknown, but the government broad arrow stamped on the reverse of the breastplate suggests that he may have been a guide, interpreter and camp assistant for surveyors looking for minerals or a route for the transcontinental railway. Another possibility is that he was a police tracker and community liaison who assisted with the distribution of rations from police depots at Coongie or Innamincka. Given the strong involvement of Aboriginal people in the cattle stations of the region, it is likely King Mulga would have also had superior stock-working skills.

records.title: Aboriginal Land Rights, Tasmania
places: Australia (Place made)
Tasmania, Australia (Associated place)
records.physical_description: Yellow polyester cotton t-shirt with "Aboriginal Land Rights" and a map of Tasmania printed on its front surface.
records.significance_statement:
The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre No 1 collection consists of three  t-shirts. A yellow  t-shirt has a map of Tasmania with ‘ABORIGINAL LAND RIGHTS’ printed on the front surface. A white t-shirt has the slogan "I / STAND / ON MY / LAND" printed on the front in black. The slogan of an Aboriginal boy wearing a cap and holding a football is superimposed on a black and white photographic image in the shape of Tasmania. A red polyester cotton t-shirt has "TASSIE / KOORIES / ARE OK / BY ME!" printed on the front with a photographic image of a group of Aboriginal people including a woman and five children. 

The Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre (TAC), established in 1973, formerly the Tasmanian Aboriginal Information Service, commenced to petition the Tasmanian Parliament in 1977 with what became known as the Aboriginal Land Claim.  The t-shirts in this collection are associated with the land claim petition and were purchased in 1990 for inclusion in the NHC.  The timing of their purchase also coincided with the establishment of the Aboriginal Provisional Government, an organisation which seeks sovereignty, land rights and self-determination for all Aboriginal Australians.  In 1995, following years of lobbying by the Aboriginal community, the Tasmanian government passed the Aboriginal Lands Act, which acknowledged the dispossession of, and sought reconciliation with, Tasmanian Aboriginal People, by returning twelve parcels of land of ‘historic and cultural significance’.  The Act provided for an elected Aboriginal Land Council to own and sustainably manage these lands. Aboriginal activist Michael Mansell later pointed out that the land returned comprised under 0.001 percent of Tasmania.

records.title: Georgy, Mudgee Police man breastplate
places: Mudgee, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)
records.description: A crescent shaped, gold coloured breastplate engraved with the words 'TOMMY MURA / STOCKMAN / DONNA. There are two holes pierced on either side attached to which is a chain. The front and back are discoloured.
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped breastplate which is dark in colour and engraved with the words 'Given by / Mr Whitting / GEORGY/ Mudgee Police man'. It features engravings of a soldier on horseback with two branches on either side. There are two holes on either side for attaching a chain
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a brass breastplate presented in the late 1830s to Georgy, a Wiradjuri man of the Mudgee region of New South Wales. 

By the 1830s it was common practice to present Aboriginal people perceived as local leaders with breastplates in an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. Breastplates were also presented as a reward for labour or particular acts of heroism. Georgy probably worked as a tracker for the Mounted Police Force, the members of which were recruited from the military regiments in the colony. In the 'nineteen counties' designated by the colonial government the Mounted Police became prominent, mainly for the capture of bushrangers and runaway convicts - with the help of skilled Aboriginal trackers such as Georgy. He was presented with his breastplate by Joshua John Whitting, who served as a Lieutenant in the 28th (North Gloucestershire) Regiment before joining the Mounted Police in 1836. It is possible that Georgy may have assisted Whitting in the successful investigation of a triple murder in February 1838.

records.title: Child's drawing
places: Amoonguna Aboriginal Land Trust, Amoonguna, Northern Territory, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
records.description:
This artwork is one of a series of some 3383 drawings and paintings on paper made between 1975-1977 by Aboriginal children from 70 schools across Australia. 

These artworks were collected by the Aboriginal Arts Board for potential use in 'The Aboriginal Children's History of Australia: Written and Illustrated by Australia's Aboriginal Children'. The book was published by Rigby, Adelaide in 1977. 

According to Robert Edwards, then Director of the Aboriginal Arts Board, the idea for collecting these Aboriginal Children's drawings evolved during a 1975 flight to Canberra. Serendipitously, Edwards sat next to Edward J. McGrath Jr, Director of the Hawaiian publishing firm, Island Heritage Limited. 

McGrath asked Edwards 'What do you do?' On hearing about the Aboriginal Arts Board's work with Australian Aboriginal communities, McGrath explained that he was publishing a series of Children's histories from different nations throughout the world. He produced from his briefcase a copy of 'A Child's History of Hawaii' and an exchange of ideas for a history book by Aboriginal children ensued. 

Edwards recalls that the flight was fortuitous, as he had been thinking about how to link Indigenous children into the Aboriginal Arts Board's art programs. Children's art seemed an obvious way of involving children, especially if the project could be organised through the school system.

A project to produce Children's artworks for a history book authored by Aboriginal children was subsequently proposed to the Aboriginal Arts Board, who approved and implemented the project in 1976.

Michael Gray was responsible for researching and coordinating the project, which incorporated 70 participating Aboriginal schools from all parts of Australia except Victoria and the Torres Strait.

The Aboriginal Arts Board transferred the collection of artworks to the National Museum of Australia in 1991.
records.physical_description: Drawing of two buildings and a tree with a swing. Text panel in pencil associated. Artist: Maxie Jabldjari Davis. Location: Amoongunya Settlement. Title: First day at school.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: LINK-UP (NSW) ABORIGINAL CORPORATION pass card for Peter Read, Public Officer
records.description: Pass issued to Peter Read
records.physical_description: A printed pass card that reads 'LINK-UP (NSW)/ABORIGINAL CORPORATION/Peter Read/Public Officer'. The card is incapsulated in plastic. A steel spring clasp attaches the pass card to a black woven cord, for wearing round the neck.
records.significance_statement:
The collection compirses the booklet 'The Stolen Generations; the Removal of Aboriginal Children in NSW 1883 to 1969'  written by Read and printed by the NSW Ministry of Aboriginal Affairs, a black metallic badge in the shape of Australia with 'Sorry' inscribed on it, the card that the badge was originally pinned to, and a laminated pass  'Link-Up NSW Aboriginal Corporation Peter Read Public Officer'. All the items are in good condition. 

The work of the historian Peter Read (b 1945) was a crucial element in the understanding of the nation-wide practice of the removal of children of mixed descent from Aboriginal families and communities.  It was he who connected stated government policies with the hundreds of instances of removal of children from NSW communities. Further research found the same processes at work in all states and territories. Stated government policies and formal and informal policies of other institutions such as churches aimed to remove children of mixed descent from their communities and to raise them as 'whites'. The intention was that they assimilate fully into the 'white' community and not return to their Indigenous one. This process has had an enormous effect on the Indigenous community, creating both social disruption and personal grief. The title of this booklet is the first usage of the term 'stolen generations' - a term used in Prime Minister Rudd's Apology speech in February 2008.

records.title: Chief Leckie, Windarra Tribe
places: Laverton, Western Australia, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
records.collection: Chief Leckie Windarra Tribe Breastplate collection
records.physical_description: A boomerang-shaped copper breastplate, impressed with 'CHIEF LECKIE / WINDARRA / TRIBE'. A brass chain is attached to the breastplate at two sides, by a metal ring looped through a punched hole. The copper shows oxidisation and wear.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a copper breastplate presented in the late 1890s to Chief Leckie, a Wongatha man from Windarra, who probably lived around Kanowna and Bulong in the eastern goldfields region of Western Australia. 

By the 1830s it was common practice in the eastern colonies to present Aboriginal people perceived as local leaders with breastplates in an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. Breastplates were also presented as a reward for labour or particular acts of heroism. Chief Leckie's local knowledge of gold and water sources would have been invaluable to prospectors, and to surveyors pegging out leases or the route of the railway from Kalgoorlie. Alternatively, he may mediated between Aboriginal people and miners during the numerous volatile exchanges of that time. It is possible he took his non-indigenous name from W. S. Leckie, a manager of gold mines in the Kanowna area. Unlike most other breastplates, which can be highly decorated, this relatively crude breastplate has been cut from scrap metal and stamped with surveyor's letters, and does much to infer the social and environmental conditions in which it was created. Chief Leckie's plate is also unusual in that it is associated with an industry (mining) and place (WA) where the practice of presenting breastplates was uncommon.

records.title: Billy Lambert, Holwood, Kings Plains, 1834
places: Holmwood, Kings Plains, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)
records.physical_description: Tarnished and worn metal breastplate with three holes drilled across the top (at the right hand side, left hand side and the centre). 'BILLY LAMBERT / Holwood / KINGS PLAINS / 1834' is engraved onto the surface together with an emu to the left of the text and a kangaroo to the right.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a brass breastplate presented in 1834 to Billy Lambert, a Wiradjuri (or possibly Gundungura) man living on a sheep and cattle station called 'Holwood' in the region now known as Blayney, near Bathurst in New South Wales. 

The first known indigenous person in Australia with a breastplate was Bungaree, to whom Governor Macquarie presented an inscribed metal plaque in 1815. By the 1830s it was common practice among pastoralists to present Aboriginal people perceived as local leaders with breastplates to establish their authority in the vicinity of the pastoralists' property. In return, the Aboriginal leader was expected to prevent their people from interrupting these pastoral endeavours and, where possible, to supply labour or information about the land. Breastplates were also presented in recognition of service, or as tokens of gratitude. Thus it is possible that Billy Lambert was a pastoral worker, with numerous responsibilities on the fast-growing property, who also mediated between his people and the newcomers. His breastplate is tangible evidence not only of a named individual - a rare record for an Aboriginal person in colonial Australian history - but also of his efforts to negotiate a place for himself and other Wiradjuri people in a rapidly transforming world.

records.title: Wombail Oouthenang, Chief of Shannon Vielle
places: Shannon Vielle Station, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)
records.description: Shannon Vielle was the station of J.P. Robinson.  It was located about 160 kms north of Armidale on the Mann River, northern NSW.
records.physical_description: A crescentric, slightly convex brass breastplate, obverse engraved 'WOMBAIL OOUTHENANG / CHIEF / OF SHANNON VIELLE', with a male figure on the left and woman and child on the right. The breastplate includes two holes to fit a neck chain.
records.significance_statement:
This collection is comprised of seventeen Australian Indigenous breastplates (also known as king plates or gorgets). They come from a collection accumulated by L. Richard Smith, a noted collector of medals and porcelain. The breastplates are associated with Indigenous people from Queensland, New South Wales and Western Australia.  The breastplates are all metal, of varying size, and are generally crescent shaped. Each is inscribed with the recipient's name, and many include an associated region and an honorary title such as 'king', 'queen' or 'chief'.  

During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, government authorities and settlers gave breastplates to Indigenous people for a variety of reasons. They were used as a way of selecting and identifying local elders to act as intermediaries between settlers and local Indigenous people. They were also given out in recognition of service and/or assistance (for example to Aboriginal stockmen or for saving people from ship wrecks).  As such, they are significant cross-cultural objects that document early interaction between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in different regions of Australia.  They often record the names of Indigenous people, and the station or region with which they are associated; people who are not otherwise represented in historical records. The collection is also significant in expanding the geographical scope of the National Museum's existing breastplate collection.

records.description: Edmund Milne (1861-1917) was born in England and emigrated to Queensland with his parents 19 months later. He had had personal contact with Aboriginal people throughout his life, from when he was a small boy in Queensland and, from the late 1860s, in New South Wales. This contact may have led him to recording the names of Aboriginal people associated with particular objects in his collection, at a time when this was rarely done. Milne seems to have begun actively collecting Indigenous artefacts in the early 1880s and was still acquiring objects a few months before his death in 1917. His work with the NSW Railways (1876-1917) enabled him to meet a broad range of people who facilitated his collecting and associated activities like visiting Aboriginal sites. From at least the time he lived at Orange NSW (1906-1915), and later at Ryde (1915-1917), near to Sydney city, he displayed his collection at his home. In addition to a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts, Milne's collection included artefacts from the South Pacific and prehistoric implements from Egypt, France and England. In his will dated 12 December 1916, Milne bequeathed his “Anthropological collection” to the “first Federal Museum opened in the Federal Capital”. The collection remained at Ryde until early 1931 when it was acquired by the Australian Institute of Anatomy in Canberra. It remained there until the Institute's collections were transferred to the National Museum of Australia in 1985.
records.physical_description: A crescentric brass breastplate with a hole at the edge of each horn to attach a chain. Engraved on the anterior surface is "DICKY / KING OF / CLYDE ROAD". A kangaroo is engraved on the left horn, and an emu on the right horn.

records.title: 'Snake, Aboriginal flag and Dugong 2' by Christopher Johnson
places: Lockhart River, Queensland, Australia (Place made)
records.description: "We are going hunting for dugong. Snake ... we saw a big snake crawling in the trees. Aboriginal flag ... we like to hold the Aboriginal flag ... and the Aboriginal flag is good for people because they like Aboriginal flag ... and we eat lots of dugong ... and dugong is nice to eat."  - Christopher Johnson, 2002
records.physical_description: A linocut print in black ink on white paper depicting a snake, the Aboriginal flag and a dugong, arranged with the flag at the centre, the dugong above, and the snake surrounding them in a U shape with its' head in the upper right corner. Handwritten text in pencil below the print reads 'snake, Aborigal[sic], Flag and Dugong / Chris'. The linocut is mounted under black matt-board.
records.significance_statement:
The Lockhart River State School Collection contains 67 prints made by children in years four to seven in 2002. The 51 lino prints and 16 monoprints capture a sense of life in Lockhart River from the children's perspective, particularly the beach and its importance to fishing and hunting.  Some subjects are familiar to children around Australia, such as pets, ice-cream, sporting teams and holidays.  Others are more specific to Lockhart River. The fauna of the area receives particular attention, with cassowaries, kangaroos, dugongs, black cockatoos, crocodiles, ants, snake eggs, turtles, eels and jellyfish all appearing. 

The prints were made as a part of the collaboration between the school and the Lockhart River Arts and Cultural Centre. The children took art classes at the Centre and worked with members of the Lockhart River Art Gang. The Cultural Centre was established in order to revitalise the communication of traditional Aboriginal culture of the region and create vocational opportunities for young people. The members of the Art Gang were the first generation of successful artists to emerge from Lockhart River, in the late 1990s, and the project with the school was an opportunity to introduce the next generation to their work and the potential of art as a vocation.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Carved wooden portrait of an Aboriginal man set in a timber frame
records.physical_description: Carved black-coloured wood carving in a roughly hewn tan timber frame. The high-relief sculpture presents a head and shoulders portrait of an Aboriginal man. He is portrayed as bare chested with a beard and moustache. His hair is swept up and to one side of his face and his mouth is wide open. 'R. PRENZEL 1917' is carved on the upper arm on the lower right hand side of the sculpture. There is a chain attached to a loop on either side at the rear of the frame.
records.significance_statement:
The Brideson collection consists of a carved wooden portrait depicting the head and shoulders of an Aboriginal man. The carver's signature and the date, 1917, are visible on the man's left shoulder. The portrait was carved by renowned Prussian born wood-carver Robert Wilhelm Prenzel, based on a photograph taken by Henry King, and which also inspired the cover of 'The Bulletin' in October 1891. 

The portrait reveals Robert Prenzel's mastery of wood carving skills and his pioneering use of Australian timbers. Based on an iconic image, the portrait illustrates the interest of non-Indigenous settler culture in Indigenous themes during the early twentieth century.

Donated through the Australian Government’s Cultural Gifts Program by Roger and Shirley Brideson in memory of Essie and Bob Brideson.

places: Lockhart River, Queensland, Australia (Place made)

Aboriginal flag ... we like to hold the Aboriginal flag ... and the Aboriginal flag is good for people because they like Aboriginal flag ... and we eat lots of dugong ... and dugong is nice to eat."  - Christopher Johnson, 2002
records.physical_description: A linocut print in black ink on white paper depicting a snake, the Aboriginal flag and a dugong, arranged with the snake at the centre, the flag above, and the dugong below it. Handwritten text in pencil below the print reads '[sn]ake, Aborigal[sic], Flag and Dugong 1 / Chris'. The linocut is mounted under black matt-board.
records.significance_statement:
The Lockhart River State School Collection contains 67 prints made by children in years four to seven in 2002. The 51 lino prints and 16 monoprints capture a sense of life in Lockhart River from the children's perspective, particularly the beach and its importance to fishing and hunting.  Some subjects are familiar to children around Australia, such as pets, ice-cream, sporting teams and holidays.  Others are more specific to Lockhart River. The fauna of the area receives particular attention, with cassowaries, kangaroos, dugongs, black cockatoos, crocodiles, ants, snake eggs, turtles, eels and jellyfish all appearing. 

The prints were made as a part of the collaboration between the school and the Lockhart River Arts and Cultural Centre. The children took art classes at the Centre and worked with members of the Lockhart River Art Gang. The Cultural Centre was established in order to revitalise the communication of traditional Aboriginal culture of the region and create vocational opportunities for young people. The members of the Art Gang were the first generation of successful artists to emerge from Lockhart River, in the late 1990s, and the project with the school was an opportunity to introduce the next generation to their work and the potential of art as a vocation.

records.title: William Vth, Emperor of all the Kamerukians Breastplate
places: Kameruka, New South Wales, Australia (Place of use)
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped brass breast plate with two holes in the top left and right corners. Engraved on the anterior surface is the inscription 'WILLAM Vth / EMPEROR / OF ALL THE / KAMERUKIANS'. Engraved to the left side of the inscription is a kangaroo and engraved to the right side of the inscription is an Emu.
records.significance_statement:
William of Kameruka breastplate collection comprises one Aboriginal breastplate engraved: "WILLIAM Vth/EMPEROR/OF ALL THE/KAMERUKIANS".

While the identity of William Vth remains unknown, there are at least two possibilities for the derivation of this name. He may have been named after King William IV of Great Britain who reigned between 1830 and 1837. An alternative is William was named after a coastal paddle steamer built in Australia in 1831, also ‘William IV’, that plied the Sydney-Merimbula-Eden route from at least 1843 until 1858. He may have been named William Vth to avoid confusion with the British king and the steamer. The above information and its form, suggest that this breastplate may date from the 1830s to the 1850s. The rank or title 'emperor' is known to have been used on just one other breastplate and the 'fir tree' motif is known on only five other breastplates in public collections.

records.title: Pair of short white cotton gloves worn by Aboriginal rights activist Faith Bandler
records.description:
These gloves were worn by Faith Bandler when she was campaigning for the right of Aboriginal Australians to be constitutionally and legally recognized as Australian citizens in the lead up to the 1967 Indigenous referendum. She explains why she wore these 'day' or 'town' gloves when addressing groups of white women: 

"I used to wear short white gloves. They were acceptable to the white community I came in contact with when I was campaigning for black women's rights. I wore them from 1956 until the mid-1960s.  During that period I only ever addressed white audiences.  I only had to convince them."

Faith Bandler came to national attention in 1956 when she and Pearl Gibbs founded the Aboriginal-Australian Fellowship, a political body which campaigned for citizenship rights for Aboriginal people. For many years she sat on the executive of the Federal Council for the Advancement of Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders.
records.physical_description: A pair of ladies' short white gloves, without a manufacturer's label. They have a zig zag stitch decoration and partial double fold at hem to wrist edge.
records.significance_statement:
The Faith Bandler collection consists of a pair of 1960s white gloves, which she wore while campaigning for the right of Aboriginal Australians to be constitutionally and legally recognized as Australian citizens during the 1967 referendum campaign. The short gloves, known as 'town' or 'day' gloves, are made of white cotton with a triple zigzag stitch decoration on the upper surface and stitching details around the fingers.  There is a partial double fold at the wrist edge hem.  Faith Bandler embodied the aspirations of Aboriginal Australians to be accepted as equals, and as 'one people' with white Australians. White gloves were representative of the formal dress code that was popular among middle class white women at that time.  By wearing the gloves, Bandler hoped to be taken seriously by her predominantly white female audience. 
  
The 1967 referendum on the 'Aboriginal question' was held to determine whether two references in the Australian Constitution, which discriminated against Aboriginal people, should be removed.  A well-known Aboriginal activist, Bandler was appointed New South Wales campaign director by the Federal Council for the Advancement of Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders (FCAATSI) which was the peak body that campaigned for Indigenous rights during the period leading up to the Referendum. She argued that a YES vote was a vote for equal rights for Aboriginal citizens. The 'YES' vote in the 1967 referendum did not give Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples the right to vote. This right had been legislated for Commonwealth elections in 1962, with the last State to provide Indigenous enfranchisement being Queensland in 1965.  This referendum saw the highest YES vote ever recorded in a Federal referendum, with 90.77 per cent voting for change. Because the majority of parliamentarians supported the proposed amendment, a NO case was never formulated for presentation as part of the referendum campaign.  The Museum has an expanding collection of Collaborating for Indigenous Rights material. Faith Bandler's gloves are a key part of this collection which focuses on the struggles for Indigenous civil and land rights from the late 1950s to the 1970s.

The collection comprises a broad range of objects including batiks, pokerwork carvings, paintings and pastel drawings on paper and other art and craft items, bibles and school readers in Pitjantjatjara, drawings by school children, photograph albums, videos and a small number of stone implements.

The collection is significant for the depth and range of material associated with a single Aboriginal settlement at Ernabella, now known as Pukatja, its art centre and with Deaconness Winifred Hilliard who was the Arts Advisor to Ernabella between 1954 and 1986. records.title: Aboriginal encampment, East Moree. August, 1952
places: Moree, New South Wales, Australia (Place depicted)
records.physical_description: A carbonite pencil drawing on plain artist's drawing paper. The drawing shows a scene of three shelters, Aboriginal people in the street and children playing.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of 101 sketches  drawn in 1952-53 by Noelle Sandwith, an English artist visiting Australia who was intent on drawing 'unusual subjects' and set her sights on the Australian outback.    A wide variety of groups and people within the Australian community are examined through the sketches.  These include Aboriginal people and their involvement in missions, life on the outskirts of town, incarceration and the role of the Protectorate.  Post-war immigration is represented through the involvement of Greeks and Italians running cafes in small country towns.  Community groups representing rural and outback people such as the Australian Inland Mission, Salvation Army, Country Women's Association and the Flying Doctor's Service also rate a significant mention.  Other issues and people who are explored include Afghan cameleers, social events such as rodeos and drinking, life in the shearing shed and the role of the local police to name a few.

On the recommendation of the Australian Inland Mission, Ms Sandwith set out for south-western Queensland and down the Birdsville track to Marree in South Australia.  She undertook this journey on her own, allowing her the freedom to travel where she wanted and to record the lives of people in the outback as she viewed it. Great changes occurred in Australia in the 1950s.  Society changed relatively quickly with the influx of immigrants following WWII.  Policies of assimilation were at their height and this extended to both the indigenous people of Australia and the newest groups of  immigrants.  This period of contact between the various sectors of the Australian community is one which of great interest to us today.  The sketches provide a view of outback society at this time and chronicle the relationships between various groups and people. There was great interest in the treatment of Australia's Indigenous inhabitants during this period.  The sketches provide a personal view of the perceptions of European people towards Aboriginal people.  Several of the sketches slip into caricature when dealing with Aboriginal people and this also provides us with Sandwith's view.  Several poignant comments are made regarding the lifestyle and expectations of Aboriginal people.  Whilst these seem dated now, they are powerful reminders of the attitudes which prevailed at the time of sketching.

'OLYMPIA WERKE AG. WILHELMSHAVEN / Made in Western Germany' is written on a silver plaque screwed to the back of the typewriter.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of 134 political cartoons collected under the auspices of the National Museum's 1999 Political Humour Competition.

The cartoons provide a satirical record of the major events and personalities in Australian politics in 1999.  Major topics addressed within the collection include the Goods and Services tax, the Sydney Olympics, the 'cash comment controversy' on talkback radio, the defeat of Jeff Kennett in the Victorian election, Republic referendum, the independence struggle in East Timor, racism, Aboriginal land rights and Australia's international relations.  There are a number of illustrations and caricatures of notable political figures including John Howard, Peter Costello, Jeff Kennett and Peter Reith.  The collection features works from all of Australia's major metropolitan newspapers.  Taken together the collection provides a wonderful archive of the best of Australian political cartooning in 1999.

records.title: Kungkarrangkalpa
places: Blackstone (Papulankutja Aboriginal community), Western Australia, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
Papulankutja, Western Australia, Australia (Place created)
records.description:
The Seven Sisters songline travels from the west to the east across the far Western and Central deserts. The sisters are pursued by an old man, Wati Nyiru, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by the Seven Sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. In Mrs Woods' print, one of the sisters is hiding from the man in a cave.  Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. These works are part of a Museum collection that represents episodes of the Seven Sisters story as they are written in sites along the songline that cross the Martu, Ngaanyatjarra, Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara Lands.


"When the songline reaches the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, the tone darkens and the actions of Wati Nyiru become more sinister. His obsession with the eldest sister is the major theme, and the paintings acquired relating to the Seven Sisters focus on several key events — the capture of the eldest sister, the cooking and eating of kuniya, (the carpet snake, which is a manifestation of the shape-shifter), and the transformation of the sisters into  stars. 
On the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, people are connected to sites through their kinship to the Ancestral characters who inhabit the narrative. The rituals of dance and song — inma — enact the universal meanings of the Tjukurrpa. The Seven Sisters drama unfolds along two songlines in this section. As you journey along the Kuru Ala songline to the south and Wanarn to the north. the paintings function as portals to place."
(Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p119)

"Tjayanka danced the eldest sister, Kampukurta, at Puyukuntji, a highly significant Seven Sisters healing place at Kuru Ala. When she danced the difficult part of the story of her encounter with the lustful man, she became very emotional. This is her painting of the sisters dancing at Kuru Ala. The dancing lines  in this work are the sisters nyampi nyampi (dancing) through the sand, before they rise into the sky. Tjayanka often only painted six sisters in her work — the
seventh sister is hiding in the cave, resting after her ordeal." (Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p148)
records.physical_description: A rectangular print on paper composed of two sets of deep red circles filled with other red and/or orange circles within them that are then connected with orange and red vertical lines. The vertical lines are then joined together with a red circle which are then connected to red and orange vertical lines. Joined to the end of each set of vertical lines are red circles that are printed within or on top of one another and have a red dot in the centre of them. The two sets of circles and lines are connected with nine red horizontal lines. Further connected to the design to the right are red and orange horizontal lines which meet together at a circle, the lower line then has angled vertical lines attached to it, which are then met with more horizontal lines at the right middle side of the paper. The majority of the vertical and horizontal lines are slightly curved. There are also red and orange dots featured throughout the design within and around the lines. Inscribed below the print is handwritten text in pencil which reads '3/15 Kungkarrankalpa Tjayanka Woods'.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of one painting and three limited edition screen prints on paper by Pitjantjatjara artist Tjayanka Woods (c.1920 - ). Woods works with Papulankutja Artists in Papulankutja community (or Blackstone), which is located at the foot of the Blackstone Ranges in WA approximately 60 kilometres west of the tri-state border. 

The Seven Sisters songline travels from the west to the east across the far Western and Central deserts. The sisters are pursued by an old man, Wati Nyiru, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by the Seven Sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. In Mrs Woods' paintings, one of the sisters is hiding from the man in a cave.  Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. These works are part of a Museum collection that represents episodes of the Seven Sisters story as they are written in sites along the songline that cross the Martu, Ngaanyatjarra, Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara Lands.

records.significance_statement:
The Herbert Browne collection consists of personal items belonging to Herbert Browne, an English-born musical theatre performer who established himself as the leading tenor with Australia's JC Williamson's Company in the period between the two world wars. The collection comprises Aboriginal and oriental objects, photographs, theatrical and biographical notes, theatre programs, news-clippings, correspondence, gramophone recordings, cosmetics and accessories from Browne's theatrical make-up business. 

Herbert Browne's life in Australia from the age of twenty six reads like a history of Australian popular entertainment, with its ups and downs, its preoccupations and its relationship to wider trends in aesthetics and material culture in Australian life. Browne's interests in objects were tethered to the entertainment industry and the wider social world in which he operated. Browne's travels across the Nullabor with JC Williamson's found expression through his collections of Aboriginal artefacts, his films and photograph albums. His Aboriginal objects and associated images provide rare glimpses into the way urban Australians encountered remote Aboriginal culture. They also document his relationship with the legendary Daisy Bates, from whom he acquired artefacts. Browne's other main collecting interest was with oriental objects which echoed stage roles he played in musical theatre productions. Browne's oriental and Aboriginal objects are complementary in illustrating the way respective cultures were represented in early-mid twentieth century domestic collections. The cultural items he acquired and their incorporation into the domestic sphere of the Australian home provide insights into the way Australians of that period represented the colonised world. These objects are strongly augmented by objects related to his theatrical make-up business which capture the role of cosmetics in transforming identity in theatrical performances by himself and others. The accompanying photographic and paper-based materials document his life in the theatre, his relationship with other theatrical identities and his work at the Australian Broadcasting Commission.

records.title: Portrait of an Aboriginal person holding seaweed, by Revel Cooper, 1976
records.description:
Revel Cooper's (1934-1983) art has its origins in the school of art known as the Carrolup drawings. This body of work was produced during a brief period in the late 1940 by young Aboriginal artists - including Revel Cooper - at the Carrolup Native Institution in southwest Western Australia, and was influenced by Noel White, the teacher at Carrolup. White provided the students with pastels and encouraged them to draw what they saw. Their drawings were predominantly landscapes with echoes and memories of their past lives.

This work is one of Cooper's later works.
records.physical_description: Acrylic paint on card. Head and shoulders of an Aboriginal person holding a bunch of seaweed. Signed in lower left hand corner.

records.title: Aboriginal humpy, Marree, South Australia. February 1953
places: Marree, South Australia, Australia (Place depicted)
records.physical_description: A carbonite pencil drawing on plain artist's drawing paper. The drawing shows four people and a dog sitting next to a shelter.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of 101 sketches  drawn in 1952-53 by Noelle Sandwith, an English artist visiting Australia who was intent on drawing 'unusual subjects' and set her sights on the Australian outback.    A wide variety of groups and people within the Australian community are examined through the sketches.  These include Aboriginal people and their involvement in missions, life on the outskirts of town, incarceration and the role of the Protectorate.  Post-war immigration is represented through the involvement of Greeks and Italians running cafes in small country towns.  Community groups representing rural and outback people such as the Australian Inland Mission, Salvation Army, Country Women's Association and the Flying Doctor's Service also rate a significant mention.  Other issues and people who are explored include Afghan cameleers, social events such as rodeos and drinking, life in the shearing shed and the role of the local police to name a few.

On the recommendation of the Australian Inland Mission, Ms Sandwith set out for south-western Queensland and down the Birdsville track to Marree in South Australia.  She undertook this journey on her own, allowing her the freedom to travel where she wanted and to record the lives of people in the outback as she viewed it. Great changes occurred in Australia in the 1950s.  Society changed relatively quickly with the influx of immigrants following WWII.  Policies of assimilation were at their height and this extended to both the indigenous people of Australia and the newest groups of  immigrants.  This period of contact between the various sectors of the Australian community is one which of great interest to us today.  The sketches provide a view of outback society at this time and chronicle the relationships between various groups and people. There was great interest in the treatment of Australia's Indigenous inhabitants during this period.  The sketches provide a personal view of the perceptions of European people towards Aboriginal people.  Several of the sketches slip into caricature when dealing with Aboriginal people and this also provides us with Sandwith's view.  Several poignant comments are made regarding the lifestyle and expectations of Aboriginal people.  Whilst these seem dated now, they are powerful reminders of the attitudes which prevailed at the time of sketching.

places: Adelaide, South Australia, Australia (Place collected)
records.collection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art (ATSIAA) collection no. 1
records.physical_description: A reproduction of a black and white print on paper featuring a woman carrying a young child on her back. The woman is wearing a possum skinned cloak. To the right of the woman is a young child with a dog. On the reverse handwritten ink black ink is "SECTION 1 / BEFORE THE EUROPEANS / No 1. 'ABORIGINAL WOMEN AND CHILD'. (reverse image) / W. HATHERELL / ...". The reproduction is mounted onto chipboard.
records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Aboriginal stockman's saddle
records.physical_description: A brown leather saddle with girth and stirrups attached. The saddle has a blue and orange sections of plush textile lining on the underside. There are remains of outlined embroidered motifs on the back and seat of the saddle. The pommel of the saddle has two small metal horseshoes attached. There is also a metal plate, with C shape loop, at each side of the pommel. One of them has the printed text "HILL / PATE[NT] /  TR[---?] / No. 27055 / 2.6.30".  The saddle has metal ring attachments on the upper section at the front and at the sides and lower back.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of 17 objects worn or used by Bruce Breaden in his daily work as head stockman on cattle stations in central Australia: an Akubra hat, a pair of R. M. Williams elastic-sided boots, a pair of R. M. Williams trousers, two long-sleeved shirts, a long-sleeved jumper, a synthetic belt (featuring a leather pocket knife pouch or sheath, counted as a separate object), a pocket knife, a Syd Hill Giltrow Poley saddle (with breastplate, stirrups, girth and surcingle attached), a leather quartpot holder, a leather saddlebag, a bridle, a pair of reins, a plaited fibre lead rope, a hobble chain and a branding iron. 

A Luritja man born at Tempe Downs, where he also first started work, Bruce Breaden fought for 25 years until he secured land rights over the Tempe Downs/Middleton Ponds region on behalf of his people. Breaden's stockman's kit represents the history of Aboriginal people in the cattle industry of northern Australia and their essential contribution to the development of what is now one of the nation's major exports (and a major source of national iconography). The collection also represents Breaden's personal expertise in traditional skills so vital to the industry before the advent of aerial mustering, beef roads and satellite technology.

records.title: You Are On Aboriginal Land
places: Australia (Place of production)
Uluru, Northern Territory, Australia (Place of event)
records.physical_description: A white cotton short sleeved T-shirt with a printed design of an Aboriginal flag with the yellow outline of Uluru in the centre. There is red text at the top and black text below in Aboriginal language.  In the black area of the flag is white text which reads "You Are On Aboriginal Land' and under the lower Aboriginal text reads "Commemorating the Hand Back of / Ayers Rock to Traditional Owners, 1985".
records.significance_statement:
The collection consists of a T-shirt that celebrates the 1985 hand-back of Uluru (Ayers Rock) to its traditional owners.  This is an example of popular culture that celebrates the government decision to hand back Uluru and the subsequent joint management of the Uluru Park.  The T-shirt was purchased by Brad Manera as an Uluru souvenir, and subsequently worn to show personal support for Indigenous Australians.

Recognised as a significant national icon by Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians, Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is also one of the few World Heritage properties listed for both its natural and cultural values.  On 26 October 1985, Governor General Sir Ninian Stephens presented the Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park Title Deeds back to the traditional owners, the Anangu.  The lands were leased back to the Australian Government in an effort to see the Anangu people and Parks Australia work together to jointly manage the park.  The example of Uluru joint management marks a significant moment in the history of Aboriginal protest and land right struggles, and also an important example of continuing efforts for reconciliation.

records.title: On court uniform from 1988 International Tour of all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander basketball team
records.description: Worn by Danny Morseu
records.physical_description: A singlet and short set, men's basketball uniform featuring a red, black and yellow Aboriginal flag design. The singlet features the number '15'  in yellow on the front and back. Both the singlet and shorts are made from stretchy polyester fabric.
records.significance_statement:
The collection is made up of objects spanning the four decades of Danny Morseu career as a professional basketball player and sporting champion from 1976 to 2004. The collection includes player uniforms, awards, personal documentation, photos (both personal and official event photos), limited edition publications, souvenirs, and athlete gifts from significant events that he has been a part of. Awards include the bronze medal won in the 1983 Commonwealth Games and a unique hand carved pearl shell which was awarded to Morseu in 1980 by the Torres Strait Islander community in recognition of his achievements in representing his country especially at the Moscow Olympic Games of that same year. 

Danny Morseu was the first Torres Strait Islander to represent Australia at the Olympic Games.  He played in 27 international competitions for Australia including 12 World Cup games championships and tours of Europe, Canada and USA.  Morseu played with the most influential clubs in Australia and is considered a founding player in the National Basketball League (NBL) which was established in 1979 and for which he was one of the main 'Poster Boys' promoting the sport during this period. His contribution to the sport and achievements in basketball were recognised when he was inducted into the NBL Hall of Fame in 2002. These objects represent Morseu's personal story as he progressed from state championship player to international sporting ambassador.

records.title: Aboriginal Curse
places: Sydney, New South Wales, Australia (Place of publication)
records.description: Exhibition: Bringing the House Down 1999 Entrant.
records.physical_description: Depicts white man on left and Aboriginal man on right. Captions -- white man: 'HOW WILL YOU / KNOW IF THE / CURSE ON / ELLIOTT IS / WORKING?'; Aboriginal man: 'HE'LL / COME AND / LIVE / WITH US'. Signed 'LINDSAY.' in bottom left corner. Paper marked below cartoon: 'THE AUSTRALIAN / 12 MARCH 1999 / 5cms DEEP / ABORIGINAL CURSE ON / ELLIOTT'.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of 134 political cartoons collected under the auspices of the National Museum's 1999 Political Humour Competition.

The cartoons provide a satirical record of the major events and personalities in Australian politics in 1999.  Major topics addressed within the collection include the Goods and Services tax, the Sydney Olympics, the 'cash comment controversy' on talkback radio, the defeat of Jeff Kennett in the Victorian election, Republic referendum, the independence struggle in East Timor, racism, Aboriginal land rights and Australia's international relations.  There are a number of illustrations and caricatures of notable political figures including John Howard, Peter Costello, Jeff Kennett and Peter Reith.  The collection features works from all of Australia's major metropolitan newspapers.  Taken together the collection provides a wonderful archive of the best of Australian political cartooning in 1999.

records.title: Kungkarrangkalpa
places: Blackstone (Papulankutja Aboriginal community), Western Australia, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
Papulankutja, Western Australia, Australia (Place created)
records.description: The Seven Sisters songline travels from the west to the east across the far Western and Central deserts. The sisters are pursued by an old man, Wati Nyiru, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by the Seven Sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. In Mrs Woods' paintings, one of the sisters is hiding from the man in a cave.  Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. These works are part of a Museum collection that represents episodes of the Seven Sisters story as they are written in sites along the songline that cross the Martu, Ngaanyatjarra, Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara Lands.
records.physical_description: A square print on paper composed of dark orange dots and circles arranged in vertical lines on a slight angle, against a lighter orange coloured background. Inscribed in pencil beneath the print is the text '2/15 Kungkarrankalpa III Tjayanka Woods'.

records.title: The Burning of the Aboriginal Flag: A Study of Racism in Shoalhaven
places: Nowra, New South Wales, Australia (Subject)
records.physical_description: Yellow covered bound booklet titled "The Burning of the Aboriginal Flag: A Study of Racism in Shoalhaven". The bottom part of the cover has a section of a questionnaire printed on it. The booklet has a black binding and there is typed text inside the document.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.title: Child's drawing: War - two Aboriginal and two European men fighting
places: Dhupuma College, Nhulunbuy, Northern Territory, Australia (Place created)
records.description:
This artwork is one of a series of some 3383 drawings and paintings on paper made between 1975-1977 by Aboriginal children from 70 schools across Australia. 

These artworks were collected by the Aboriginal Arts Board for potential use in 'The Aboriginal Children's History of Australia: Written and Illustrated by Australia's Aboriginal Children'. The book was published by Rigby, Adelaide in 1977. 

According to Robert Edwards, then Director of the Aboriginal Arts Board, the idea for collecting these Aboriginal Children's drawings evolved during a 1975 flight to Canberra. Serendipitously, Edwards sat next to Edward J. McGrath Jr, Director of the Hawaiian publishing firm, Island Heritage Limited. 

McGrath asked Edwards 'What do you do?' On hearing about the Aboriginal Arts Board's work with Australian Aboriginal communities, McGrath explained that he was publishing a series of Children's histories from different nations throughout the world. He produced from his briefcase a copy of 'A Child's History of Hawaii' and an exchange of ideas for a history book by Aboriginal children ensued. 

Edwards recalls that the flight was fortuitous, as he had been thinking about how to link Indigenous children into the Aboriginal Arts Board's art programs. Children's art seemed an obvious way of involving children, especially if the project could be organised through the school system.

A project to produce Children's artworks for a history book authored by Aboriginal children was subsequently proposed to the Aboriginal Arts Board, who approved and implemented the project in 1976.

Michael Gray was responsible for researching and coordinating the project, which incorporated 70 participating Aboriginal schools from all parts of Australia except Victoria and the Torres Strait.

The Aboriginal Arts Board transferred the collection of artworks to the National Museum of Australia in 1991.
records.physical_description: Depicts two people shooting two Aborigines who have spears. Artist: Unknown. Location: Nhulunbuy, NT.

records.title: Aboriginal mission station, Moree, N.S.W. Cabin interior. August, 1952
places: Moree, New South Wales, Australia (Place depicted)
records.physical_description: A carbonite pencil drawing on plain artist's drawing paper. The drawing shows a young child sitting inside a room.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of 101 sketches  drawn in 1952-53 by Noelle Sandwith, an English artist visiting Australia who was intent on drawing 'unusual subjects' and set her sights on the Australian outback.    A wide variety of groups and people within the Australian community are examined through the sketches.  These include Aboriginal people and their involvement in missions, life on the outskirts of town, incarceration and the role of the Protectorate.  Post-war immigration is represented through the involvement of Greeks and Italians running cafes in small country towns.  Community groups representing rural and outback people such as the Australian Inland Mission, Salvation Army, Country Women's Association and the Flying Doctor's Service also rate a significant mention.  Other issues and people who are explored include Afghan cameleers, social events such as rodeos and drinking, life in the shearing shed and the role of the local police to name a few.

On the recommendation of the Australian Inland Mission, Ms Sandwith set out for south-western Queensland and down the Birdsville track to Marree in South Australia.  She undertook this journey on her own, allowing her the freedom to travel where she wanted and to record the lives of people in the outback as she viewed it. Great changes occurred in Australia in the 1950s.  Society changed relatively quickly with the influx of immigrants following WWII.  Policies of assimilation were at their height and this extended to both the indigenous people of Australia and the newest groups of  immigrants.  This period of contact between the various sectors of the Australian community is one which of great interest to us today.  The sketches provide a view of outback society at this time and chronicle the relationships between various groups and people. There was great interest in the treatment of Australia's Indigenous inhabitants during this period.  The sketches provide a personal view of the perceptions of European people towards Aboriginal people.  Several of the sketches slip into caricature when dealing with Aboriginal people and this also provides us with Sandwith's view.  Several poignant comments are made regarding the lifestyle and expectations of Aboriginal people.  Whilst these seem dated now, they are powerful reminders of the attitudes which prevailed at the time of sketching.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: The Seven Sisters
places: Blackstone (Papulankutja Aboriginal community), Western Australia, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
Papulankutja, Western Australia, Australia (Place created)
records.description:
The Seven Sisters songline travels from the west to the east across the far Western and Central deserts. The sisters are pursued by an old man, Wati Nyiru, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by the Seven Sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. In Mrs Woods' paintings, one of the sisters is hiding from the man in a cave.  Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. 

"When the songline reaches the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, the tone darkens and the actions of Wati Nyiru become more sinister. His obsession with the eldest sister is the major theme, and the paintings acquired relating to the Seven Sisters focus on several key events — the capture of the eldest sister, the cooking and eating of kuniya, (the carpet snake, which is a manifestation of the shape-shifter), and the transformation of the sisters into  stars. 
On the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, people are connected to sites through their kinship to the Ancestral characters who inhabit the narrative. The rituals of dance and song — inma — enact the universal meanings of the Tjukurrpa. The Seven Sisters drama unfolds along two songlines in this section. As you journey along the Kuru Ala songline to the south and Wanarn to the north. the paintings function as portals to place."
(Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p119)

"Tjayanka danced the eldest sister, Kampukurta, at Puyukuntji, a highly significant Seven Sisters healing place at Kuru Ala. When she danced the difficult part of the story of her encounter with the lustful man, she became very emotional. This is her painting of the sisters dancing at Kuru Ala. The dancing lines  in this work are the sisters nyampi nyampi (dancing) through the sand, before they rise into the sky. Tjayanka often only painted six sisters in her work — the
seventh sister is hiding in the cave, resting after her ordeal." (Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p148)
records.physical_description: An acrylic painting on canvas featuring three bulbous figures composed of white, red, blue, pink and purple dots, lines and circles. Each one of the figures has a circle at the top and bottom end of the painting and are joined together with multi-coloured lines. The three figures are further surrounded by other coloured lines within a black painted frame. Also inscribed in black paint on the outer left edge of the painting is the text '10 - 160 TJAYANKA WOODS PAPULANKUTJA ARTISTS BLACKSTONE'.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of one painting and three limited edition screen prints on paper by Pitjantjatjara artist Tjayanka Woods (c.1920 - ). Woods works with Papulankutja Artists in Papulankutja community (or Blackstone), which is located at the foot of the Blackstone Ranges in WA approximately 60 kilometres west of the tri-state border. 

The Seven Sisters songline travels from the west to the east across the far Western and Central deserts. The sisters are pursued by an old man, Wati Nyiru, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by the Seven Sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. In Mrs Woods' paintings, one of the sisters is hiding from the man in a cave.  Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. These works are part of a Museum collection that represents episodes of the Seven Sisters story as they are written in sites along the songline that cross the Martu, Ngaanyatjarra, Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara Lands.

records.title: Spearthrower collected by Daisy Bates from Aboriginal visitors to her Ooldea camp
records.physical_description: A spear-thrower with a handle that has ruminants of resin on it. The opposite end has a spear tail-rest peg bound onto it with sinew and resin. Longitudinal splits along one side have been pulled together at a hole with sinew. The front half of the concave upper surface is engraved with a zig zag pattern of four parallel lines, and the back half contains two squares containing zig zag lines, and one rectangle containing diagonal lines. The surface is covered with longitudinal adze marks and there are two areas bearing traces of red ochre. The convex underside is mostly covered with diagonal adze marks but there is also a band of longitudinal marks near the rest end.
records.significance_statement:
The Herbert Browne collection consists of personal items belonging to Herbert Browne, an English-born musical theatre performer who established himself as the leading tenor with Australia's JC Williamson's Company in the period between the two world wars. The collection comprises Aboriginal and oriental objects, photographs, theatrical and biographical notes, theatre programs, news-clippings, correspondence, gramophone recordings, cosmetics and accessories from Browne's theatrical make-up business. 

Herbert Browne's life in Australia from the age of twenty six reads like a history of Australian popular entertainment, with its ups and downs, its preoccupations and its relationship to wider trends in aesthetics and material culture in Australian life. Browne's interests in objects were tethered to the entertainment industry and the wider social world in which he operated. Browne's travels across the Nullabor with JC Williamson's found expression through his collections of Aboriginal artefacts, his films and photograph albums. His Aboriginal objects and associated images provide rare glimpses into the way urban Australians encountered remote Aboriginal culture. They also document his relationship with the legendary Daisy Bates, from whom he acquired artefacts. Browne's other main collecting interest was with oriental objects which echoed stage roles he played in musical theatre productions. Browne's oriental and Aboriginal objects are complementary in illustrating the way respective cultures were represented in early-mid twentieth century domestic collections. The cultural items he acquired and their incorporation into the domestic sphere of the Australian home provide insights into the way Australians of that period represented the colonised world. These objects are strongly augmented by objects related to his theatrical make-up business which capture the role of cosmetics in transforming identity in theatrical performances by himself and others. The accompanying photographic and paper-based materials document his life in the theatre, his relationship with other theatrical identities and his work at the Australian Broadcasting Commission.

records.title: 'Chainsaw Gunduy' (cassowary) by Leonard Andy and artists of Girringun Aboriginal Arts, 2015
records.physical_description: A cassowary sculpture made of recycled chainsaw parts, painted silver in colour. The body consists of flat metal sheets and other mechanical parts cut in different shapes and attached together, and has a hollow centre.
records.significance_statement:
The collection comprises a sculpture titled 'Chainsaw Gunduy' created by Leonard Andy in 2015. Andy was the concept creator and lead artist of the sculpture, with the support of George Beeron, Nephi Denham, Phillip Denham, Chris Kennedy, Shannon Solomon and Alan Tobanne from Girringun Aboriginal Arts. 

The Gunduy (cassowary) is the iconic and endangered flightless bird of the Wet Tropics region, and holds great spiritual and environmental significance for the artist. Andy has worked with CSIRO scientists in the effort to save this endangered bird and its delicate habitat. Andy's work also reponds to the effect of colonisation on his country, with destruction that is both spiritual and environmental. Much of Andy's traditional country has become suburban development with the introduction of non-Indigenous plants and animals, and the presence of people from other regions of Australia, who have little awareness of the local Aboriginal culture or of the conflict and violence of colonial history. For many years, Andy worked as a cultural guide in Far North Queensland to communicate his culture to tourists and residents.

records.title: Olympia typewriter used to type Aboriginal land claims
places: West Germany (Place made)
records.physical_description: A metal and plastic 'Olympia' brand typewriter with an attached case. The typewriter has a grey plastic base and a bone coloured body with green turning knobs. 'OLYMPIA WERKE AG. WILHELMSHAVEN / Made in Western Germany' is written on a silver plaque screwed to the back of the typewriter. The attached case is dark brown and an off white colour with a brown handle and a lock. The case is hinged. A layer of blue felt lies over the typewriter.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.
