records.collection: Western Desert Nganampa Walytja Palyantjaku Tjutaku Aboriginal Corporation (Purple House) collection
records.physical_description: A red, black and yellow Aboriginal flag. It is made from polyester and is machine sewn except for the yellow circle in the centre which has been applied with adhesive.
records.significance_statement:
The Western Desert Nganampa Walytja Palyantjaku Tjutaku Aboriginal Corporation (Purple House) collection consists of a patient dialysis chair; a handpainted sign, 'Purple House Renal'; a handmade Aboriginal flag; and handknitted rug. 

The dialysis chair and rug in this collection have been used by documented Pintupi dialysis patients at 'Purple House' in Kintore. This centre is significant because it was the first remote community to offer haemodialysis to patients 'on country' through their own fundraising efforts. The sign and flag are important because they mark the tenth anniversary, in September 2014, of the opening of 'Purple House' in Kintore. At the anniversary celebrations, the original hand painted sign, 'Purple House Renal', was replaced by a new professionally painted sign, ' Yari Yari Zimran Tjampitjinpa Dialysis Centre', in honour of the man whose vision the centre was.

records.description:
Revel Cooper's (1934-1983) art has its origins in the school of art known as the Carrolup drawings. This body of work was produced by young Aboriginal artists - including Revel Cooper - at the Carrolup Native Institution in southwest Western Australia during a brief period in the late 1940s, and was influenced by Noel White, the teacher at Carrolup. White provided the students with pastels and encouraged them to draw what they saw. Their drawings were predominantly landscapes with echoes and memories of their past lives.

This work is one of Cooper's later works.

records.title: Kinchela Boys Home gate, 1950s
places: Kempsey, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)
records.description:
This is one of the original gates from Kinchela Aboriginal Boys Training Home near Kempsey in northern New South Wales. This gate, along with its pair, formed the front gates of the home and was replaced and discarded in the 1950s.

At the time, Kinchela was promoted as a place of success in assimilating its residents into the European lifestyle and a place that took great care of its residents. However, the experience of its residents was very different. The home, especially in its early years, was notorious for its cruelty, abuse and violence.

When the home closed in 1970, pressure from Aboriginal leaders ensured that the land passed into Aboriginal ownership. It now belongs to the Kempsey Local Aboriginal Land Council.
records.physical_description: A metal gate panel with welded metal letters at the top which read 'BOYS. HOME'. Remnants of wire mesh are attached to the tubular upright components of the gate, which are on the outer edges and in the centre.The gate was painted white and has rusted in several places..
records.significance_statement:
This gate is one of a pair that originally formed the front gates of Kinchela Aboriginal Boys Training Home, located near Kempsey in northern New South Wales. Made from heavy metal, it is the left side of the gate and has the words 'Boys Home' across the top. The gates were replaced in the 1950s. In the 1990s this gate was found by a community member near the Macleay River, where it was presumably thrown, and kept by a local Dunguddi Elder. It was donated to the Museum by the Kinchela Boys to ensure the story of Kinchela and the broader story of the Stolen Generations will never be forgotten.

Kinchela Aboriginal Boys Training Home opened in 1924 and closed in 1970. It housed Aboriginal boys aged from five to fifteen who had been removed from their families under the Aborigines Protection Amending Act No. 2, 1915. The aim of the home was not just to train boys for employment, but also to dissociate them from family, community and culture, with the intention to assimilate them into the 'white' population. The home, especially in its early years, was notorious for its cruelty. It was never a safe place. Former residents have suffered all their lives from the violence and abuse they experienced in the home, and from the psychological pain of being denied both an Aboriginal and a 'white' identity. They suffered the loss of family relationships and of their cultural birthright, which for some could never be retrieved. For many, however, the bond of being a Kinchela Boy has been a sustaining relationship in the world beyond Kinchela.

places: Milingimbi, Central Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
Milingimbi, Central Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
records.description:
This artwork is one of a series of some 3383 drawings and paintings on paper made between 1975-1977 by Aboriginal children from 70 schools across Australia. 

These artworks were collected by the Aboriginal Arts Board for potential use in 'The Aboriginal Children's History of Australia: Written and Illustrated by Australia's Aboriginal Children'. The book was published by Rigby, Adelaide in 1977. 

According to Robert Edwards, then Director of the Aboriginal Arts Board, the idea for collecting these Aboriginal Children's drawings evolved during a 1975 flight to Canberra. Serendipitously, Edwards sat next to Edward J. McGrath Jr, Director of the Hawaiian publishing firm, Island Heritage Limited. 

McGrath asked Edwards 'What do you do?' records.title: Head and shoulders of an Aboriginal man and a European man, by Revel Cooper, 1976
records.description:
Revel Cooper's (1934-1983) art has its origins in the school of art known as the Carrolup drawings. This body of work was produced by young Aboriginal artists - including Revel Cooper - at the Carrolup Native Institution in southwest Western Australia during a brief period in the late 1940s, and was influenced by Noel White, the teacher at Carrolup. White provided the students with pastels and encouraged them to draw what they saw. Their drawings were predominantly landscapes with echoes and memories of their past lives.

This work is one of Cooper's later works.

records.title: Koorakookoo...Free newspaper published by NSW Aboriginal Land Council
places: Parliament House, Sydney, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia (Place of event)
records.physical_description: Black and white four page newspaper titled "Koorakookoo...Free". The headline on the front page reads "LAND RIGHTS CALL IN NSW PARLIAMENT". The paper was published by the NSW Aboriginal Land Council.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Quilt titled 'Aboriginal Culture: Wetland Resources' by Pat Forster of the WA Inspired Art Quilters
places: Perth, Western Australia, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
records.description:
This quilt is part of a set of 16 titled ‘Noongar Country, Wetland Glimpses: Wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain’. The set was created in 2017/2018 by the WA Inspired Art Quilters, a group of eight Western Australian women whose purpose is to make art quilts for public exhibition. The group members are: Hilary Arber, Roberta Chantler, Meg Cowey, Pat Forster, Elizabeth Humphreys, Stephanie Knudsen, Stella King and Denise Mallon.

Each quilt in this set draws on a particular aspect of the wetland landscape, and is based on field observations and research of historical texts. A booklet describing the references and quotes that have inspired each quilt, also makes reference to the main theme of each quilt, including the featured plant and animal species, their Noongar names, and other information relevant to traditional Noongar culture. Consultation with Noongar groups has also been undertaken, including:

•	appraisal by the Shire of Cockburn Aboriginal Reference Group, Perth, June 19 2018
•	viewing by Noongar elders at the Western Australian Museum, Albany, July 9 2018
•	viewing by Noongar elder women of the City of Perth, August 2018, arranged by the City of Perth

A letter of response from the Shire of Cockburn Aboriginal Reference Group (ARG), stated “The ARG for the City of Cockburn would like to provide their support on the WA Inspired Art Quilters. The ARG can see that a lot of research with recognised, referenced Aboriginal resources, heart and spirit went into producing these quilts.

“The ARG are pleased to know that the quilts will be exhibited throughout the Noongar country and nationally for upcoming events and hope that wider community can find the beautiful, cultural significance in the quilts as the ARG will continue to do.”

This quilts have been exhibited at the following venues:

•	Western Australian Museum, Albany, July 8 - 29, 2018
•	City of Perth Library, August 21 - November 19, 2018
•	World Wetlands Day Conference, Cockburn, WA, February 2019
•	Australasian Quilt Convention, Melbourne, 11 -14 April 2019
•	Rockingham Central Library 29 April to 24 May 2019
records.physical_description: A quilt featuring a circle superimposed on an indigenous designed fabric. Within the circle is the text 'Aboriginal Culture / Wetlands Resources / freshwater plant foods plant medicines / animal foods animal skins / fibre for huts and vessels / wood for fuel tools and weapons / gum resin / tinder minerals / shade / shelter'. Other techniques include; machine applique, hand embroidery, and hand and machine quilting.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a set of 16 quilts titled ‘Noongar Country, Wetland Glimpses: Wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain’. The set was created by the WA Inspired Art Quilters, a group of quilters in Perth, Western Australia. They have been displayed at various public venues during the period 2018-19. The set was designed in a spirit of reconciliation, and to raise awareness of the great cultural significance the wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain hold for the Whadjuk Noongar people, the Traditional Owners of the region.

At the time of European settlement, the area that is now the Perth metropolitan region featured a network of wetlands that ran roughly parallel with the coast both north and south of the Swan River along the Swan Coastal Plain. These wetlands provided food, fresh water, raw materials and spiritual nourishment for the Whadjuk Noongar, whose connections with the country are maintained through songs and stories. Unable to recognise the great significance of these wetlands, the early settlers drained and built over a large percentage of them, severing many of the cultural connections that had existed for millennia, and destroying the habitat of countless plants and animals. Today, the surviving wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain are once again seen as places of high cultural and spiritual value, both as a refuge for endangered plants and animals, as well as a sanctuary for people in an increasingly urbanised landscape.

records.title: Breastplate presented to the Yandruwandha people of Cooper Creek
places: Innamincka, South Australia, Australia (Associated place)
Cooper Creek, South Australia, Australia (Associated place)
records.physical_description: A shallow crescent-shaped brass breastplate with a hole at each corner, engraved with text that reads 'Presented to / [blank] / by the Exploration Committee of Victoria for the / Humanity shewn to the Explorers / Burke, Wills & King / 1861'.
records.significance_statement:
The James de Pury collection comprises a brass, shallow crescent breastplate, two boomerangs made by the Yandruwandha people and a set of photographs taken by James de Pury of the inhabitants and landscape around Innamincka in Central Australia, in the 1920s and 1930s. The breastplate was presented to the Yandruwandha people of Cooper Creek in 1862 by Alfred Howitt, leader of the Relief Expedition sent to find the explorers Burke and Wills. It is engraved: Presented to [blank] By the Expoloration Committee of Victoria For the Humanity shewn to the Explorers Burke, Wills and King 1861.

The Victorian Exploring Expedition, later known as the Burke and Wills Expedition, remains one of the most celebrated journeys of the 'heroic era' of Australian land exploration. The huge expedition led by Robert O'Hara Burke with some twenty-one tonnes of equipment and supplies left Royal Park in Melbourne on 20 August, 1860. Burke reached his goal, crossing the continent but he and William John Wills and John Gray died on the return. The sole survivor of the Gulf party, John King was cared for by the Yandruwandha until found by Howitt's relief party in September 1861. The breastplate is one of very few objects that documents cross cultural appreciation of the Aboriginal people in caring and imparting survival skills to the many explorers of the era ignorant of the skills necessary to survive in the bush.

The National Historical Collection has a small number of iconic items relating to the Burke and Wills expedition. These include a water bottle believed to have belonged to Burke and collected from his camp by Alfred Howitt and a gold pocket watch used by William John Wills on the expedition. The James de Pury collection complements these items and extends the scope of collections relating to the expedition by adding items that relate to the indigenous inhabitants of the area and their interactions with the explorers Burke and Wills.

records.title: Breastplate 'Gallawang King of Delta, 1893
places: Delta Downs Station, Normanton, Queensland, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
Delta Downs Station, Normanton, Queensland, Australia (Place worn)
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped, brass breastplate with a circular detail above the centre, and with a hole at the apex of each of the two horns. On the anterior surface, text is stamped around the circular detail which reads '1893' and on the cresecnt section which reads 'GALLAWANG / KING OF DELTA'.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a brass breastplate, eight sepia photographs, a cardboard box and some archival material. The plate was presented to Gallawang, an Aboriginal man who was the head stockman at Delta Downs Station (or Delta Station) in 1893, by the station manager, James Alexander Moir. On the top edge of the plate the year '1893' has been stamped into the metal. On the body of the breastplate 'GALLAWANG / KING OF DELTA' has been stamped. The photographs depict the homestead, the Moir family and Aboriginal workers. 

Breastplates are a tangible record of relationships between individual settlers and Aboriginal people around mainland Australia. They were frequently presented to recognise the 'Chief' or 'King' of a 'tribe', which was often an attempt to aid peaceable settlement. They also often recognise service, such as on pastoral properties like Delta Downs where by the 1880s most of the stockmen were Aboriginal. Delta Downs is located 80 kilometres north of Normanton, on the Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Queensland, on the land of the Kurtjar people.

records.title: 'We want to change the way Aboriginal people look at us', The Fred Hollows Foundation
records.physical_description: A laminated black and white poster featuring three black and white photographs and text. Printed white text on the black background at the top reads 'We want to / change the way / Aboriginal people / look at us'. Three black and white photographs from left to right feature a close up of an eye with trachoma, Fred Hollows examining a patient, and a close up of a healthy eye. Below the photographs is an extended text box, featuring The Fred Hollows Foundation logo at the bottom right.
records.significance_statement:
The Fred Hollows Foundation collection consists of two optical trial lens frames, a cased binocular indirect ophthalmoscope with instruction manual, a cased set of trial glass lenses and metal frames, and two storage boxes. The equipment was used during the National Trachoma and Eye Health Program (NTEHP) that was established by Professor Fred Hollows AC from 1976-1979. The medical instruments are in good condition, while the lenses case and equipment boxes show substantial sign of wear. The collection also consists of a portrait of Fred Hollows and two promotional posters published by The Fred Hollows Foundation. 

Professor Fred Hollows AC (1929-1993) was an ophthalmologist who believed in equality for all, particularly in eye health. He dedicated his life to helping disadvantaged communities in Australia and overseas by treating avoidable blindness, mostly caused by trachoma or cataracts. Hollows' commitment to indigenous health in Australia was a pioneering step in bridging the gap between the health of indigenous and non-indigenous Australians.  The Fred Hollows Foundation, established in 1992, carried out Hollows' plans for intraocular lens (IOL) manufacturing facilities in Eritrea, Nepal and Vietnam, where locally-trained doctors perform cataract surgery with this locally-made, high-quality, low-cost device.  The Foundation continues Fred Hollows' work to restore sight to millions of people in Australia, Africa, Asia and the Pacific.

records.significance_statement:
The collection consists of one artwork, Fanny, Mary and the Cross, by Joel Birnie. The work was offered to the National Museum of Australia by the Tandanya National Aboriginal Cultural Institute on behalf of the artist. The work is an acrylic painting on board, and is in good condition.

The work features Fanny Cochrane Smith and her daughter Mary.  It is a personal reflection for Joel Birnie of his Grandmother and Great-Grandmother, and a comment on the broader issues surrounding the history of Fanny Cochrane Smith and Tasmania's Indigenous peoples. Fanny, Mary and The Cross was part of the travelling exhibition, Native Title Business: Contemporary Indigenous Art, which toured throughout Australia from 2002-05. In his work, Birnie has addressed the issue of Native Title in Tasmania, and within that context has interwoven interpretations of his own Indigenous heritage.

records.title: Painting depicting two Aboriginal people and a dog in treed landscape, by Jack Wherra
places: Mowanjum, West Kimberley, Western Australia, Australia (Place used)
records.collection: Gwen and Wayne Masters collection no. 2
records.description: This is part of a collection of First Nations' objects and related material which Wayne and Gwen Masters acquired while working at the Mowanjum mission near Derby, during the period 1966 to 1971.
records.physical_description: A predominantly yellow and green acrylic-wash(?) painting on cardboard sourced from an apple carton, depicting two Aboriginal people who are wearing white loin cloths and a dog, set against a treed landscape. The woman is carrying a wooden container, and the man a spear and spearthrower. The painting is signed "JACK WHERRA". There is a small dented hole in the cardboard in the trunk of the small tree.
records.significance_statement:
The Gwen and Wayne Masters No2 collection consists of eighteen objects relating to the the Mowanjum mission in north-west Australia.  It is comprised of three spears with glass tipped "Kimberley poin" blades, two boomerangs, two decorated boab nuts, a wooden spindle with hair string attached, a coolamon, a turtle shell, a spear point, and two paintings, one by Jack Wherra and one by Basel Rangea, as well as two biblical texts in the Worora language and three issues of the mission 'Encounter' magazine.

Mowanjum, a Worora word meaning 'settled at last', is a remote Aboriginal community located near Derby in north-west Australia.  Members of the Worora, Ngarinyin, and Wunumbul clan groups form the majority of Mowanjum's residents, who were brought together by missionaries in the early twentieth century at the Kunmunya Presbyterian Mission and were forcibly moved across three different locations before arriving at the present site.  Since the departure of the missionaries in the 1970s, Mowanjum has operated as an Indigenous corporation with an elected governing committee. The collection was assembled by the Masters whilst working on the Mowanjum mission during the late 1960s and early 1970s and is related to a collection that they donated to the National Museum in 1982. The collection reflects the diverse range of Indigenous objects manufactured for sale by mission residents of Mowanjum during the latter twentieth century, as well as the collecting interests of Mowanjum mission workers of the time. The objects were highly prized by the Masters. The cultural practices reflected in these objects include the maintenance of language, as evidenced by the bible translations, the maintenance of traditional hunting practices as evidenced by the spears, boomerangs and hair string, and the maintenance of story telling traditions as evidenced by the carved boab nuts and the painting, believed to have been done in the Broome gaol sometime between 1966 and 1970.

records.title: Aurukun Christmas card featuring Aboriginal canoe (1960s)
places: Aurukun, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, Australia (Place depicted)
records.description: Sold by Deaconess Winifred Hilliard to Janet Norris.
records.physical_description: A Christmas card from Aurukun printed on white glossy paper featuring a landscape photograph on the front, depicting a man and two children inside a wooden canoe on a beach next to a body of water, with a tree behind them and bush across the water. The paper is folded into quarters, with black text printed inside the first fold of the card reading 'NATIVE CANOE AT AURUKUN / PRESBYTERIAN MISSION, NORTH QUEENSLAND.' on the bottom of the left side, next to an illustration of a lizard beneath a plant. On the right side is black text reading '"Love came down at Christmas" / CHRISTMAS AND / NEW YEAR GREETINGS'.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises arts and crafts sold by the late Deaconess Winifred Hilliard to Janet Norris, a fellow member of the Trinity Presbyterian Church, Camberwell. Winifred maintained a craft program at Ernabella Mission from the 1950s when Janet was a member of the Presbyterian Women’s Missionary Union at Trinity. The role of the group was to raise money to fund craft activities and support the various missions. They did this by selling Christmas cards and items made by the Aboriginal peoples of Ernabella, in particular.

As a collection, these items represent the diversity of arts and crafts produced at such missions during the 1950s and 1960s. In addition to colourful Christmas cards, featuring reproductions of rock art, photographs of Aboriginal families, and abstract designs in Ernabella style, the collection contains two 'walka' paintings used for Christmas card designs and four examples of pokerwork from Ernabella. The collection also includes an early example of a batik by Tjunkaya Tayapa. These items reflect the Norris family’s strong support for the mission at Ernabella and other Presbyterian missions, as well as the reach of Winifred’s work in promoting Ernabella arts and crafts over the decades she lived there.

records.title: Commemorating 25 years of Aboriginal Citizenship
places: Lovett Tower, Woden Town Centre, Phillip, Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, Australia (Place collected)
records.collection: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art (ATSIAA) collection no. 1
records.physical_description: A colour poster featuring a central yellow circle containing three figures, a man, women and child. There is yellow text above and below the circle which is surrounded by a snake on a red background and white boarder.  Some of the text reads "COMMEMORATING 25 YEARS / OF ABORIGINAL CITIZENSHIP". At the bottom is black typed text within the white boarder some of which reads "Artwork by Muriel Van Der By for the 'Through Our Eyes' project". The poster is under glass with a metal frame painted black.
records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Scarf by Nyukana (Daisy) Baker, about 1975, Ernabella SA
places: Ernabella, South Australia, Australia (Place made)
records.physical_description: A square batik textile length in the colours of turquoise, green and cream. The design consists of a large stylised flower with four pointed corners. The name "Nyukana" appears on one corner. There are two tears that are stitched and opposite each other near the edges of object.
records.significance_statement:
Winifred Hilliard collection no. 2 comprises a wide range of art and craft items including batik fabrics and clothing, pokerwork animals, acrylic paintings and children's drawings.

Ernabella Arts is significant as one of the longest running Aboriginal art centres. Started in 1949, its artists are mainly women although men have been participating at an increasing rate of late. Over the years, many product lines have been attempted with batik being one of the most successful. It was introduced by Winifred Hilliard who was arts co-ordinator at Ernabella between 1954 and 1986. She is fondly remembered there largely due to role of assisting the artists rather than directing them what forms of art and craft to produce. In terms of the history of indigenous art and craft production in Australia both Ernabella Arts and Deaconess Hilliard hold significant postions.

records.title: Sambo [crossed out], King of Mount Morris, W.M. Hill
places: Charleville, Queensland, Australia (Place made)
Mount Morris, Queensland, Australia (Associated place)
records.description: Mount Morris Station was taken up in the early 1870's and is located on the Langlo River about 120kms NW of Charleville.  It had a large community of aborigines from the beginning of its formation, and its King then was Sambo.This plate was made by Mr Hill who was a well known blacksmith in Charleville in the 1870's. After Sambo's death the plate was passed onto Charley, hence name of Sambo was scratched off.  H.E, Parry-Okeden was the proprietor.
records.physical_description: A brass, crescentric breastplate without chain, obverse engraved 'SAMBO [crossed out] / KING OF / MOUNT MORRIS /  W.M. Hill', with an emu on the left and a kangaroo on the right, including two holes to fit a neck chain.
records.significance_statement:
This collection is comprised of seventeen Australian Indigenous breastplates (also known as king plates or gorgets). They come from a collection accumulated by L. Richard Smith, a noted collector of medals and porcelain. The breastplates are associated with Indigenous people from Queensland, New South Wales and Western Australia.  The breastplates are all metal, of varying size, and are generally crescent shaped. Each is inscribed with the recipient's name, and many include an associated region and an honorary title such as 'king', 'queen' or 'chief'.  

During the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, government authorities and settlers gave breastplates to Indigenous people for a variety of reasons. They were used as a way of selecting and identifying local elders to act as intermediaries between settlers and local Indigenous people. They were also given out in recognition of service and/or assistance (for example to Aboriginal stockmen or for saving people from ship wrecks).  As such, they are significant cross-cultural objects that document early interaction between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in different regions of Australia.  They often record the names of Indigenous people, and the station or region with which they are associated; people who are not otherwise represented in historical records. The collection is also significant in expanding the geographical scope of the National Museum's existing breastplate collection.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: Untitled child's drawing by Bryan Nemarluk showing an Aboriginal man about to axe a white man lying wounded on the ground
records.description:
This artwork is one of a series of some 3383 drawings and paintings on paper made between 1975-1977 by Aboriginal children from 70 schools across Australia. 

These artworks were collected by the Aboriginal Arts Board for potential use in 'The Aboriginal Children's History of Australia: Written and Illustrated by Australia's Aboriginal Children'. The book was published by Rigby, Adelaide in 1977. 

According to Robert Edwards, then Director of the Aboriginal Arts Board, the idea for collecting these Aboriginal Children's drawings evolved during a 1975 flight to Canberra. Serendipitously, Edwards sat next to Edward J. McGrath Jr, Director of the Hawaiian publishing firm, Island Heritage Limited. 

McGrath asked Edwards 'What do you do?' On hearing about the Aboriginal Arts Board's work with Australian Aboriginal communities, McGrath explained that he was publishing a series of Children's histories from different nations throughout the world. He produced from his briefcase a copy of 'A Child's History of Hawaii' and an exchange of ideas for a history book by Aboriginal children ensued. 

Edwards recalls that the flight was fortuitous, as he had been thinking about how to link Indigenous children into the Aboriginal Arts Board's art programs. Children's art seemed an obvious way of involving children, especially if the project could be organised through the school system.

A project to produce Children's artworks for a history book authored by Aboriginal children was subsequently proposed to the Aboriginal Arts Board, who approved and implemented the project in 1976.

Michael Gray was responsible for researching and coordinating the project, which incorporated 70 participating Aboriginal schools from all parts of Australia except Victoria and the Torres Strait.

The Aboriginal Arts Board transferred the collection of artworks to the National Museum of Australia in 1991.
records.physical_description: Acrylic paint, felt-tipped pen on paper. Aboriginal man about to axe a white man, wounded man lying on ground. Hills & trees. Artist: Bryan Nemarluk. Untitled.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

records.title: 'An Aboriginal Perspective from the Lillipilli Tree', Gordon Syron, 2005
places: Port Jackson, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia (Place depicted)
records.physical_description: An oil painting on linen showing a scene of lush green vegetation surrounding black coloured human figures [Aborginal people] as they observe from a distance white coloured human figures wearing red coats hoisting a British flag. Painted over the entire scene are four metal chains running vertically from top to bottom. The signature 'SYRON 2005' can be seen in the bottom right corner.The back of the painting has the word 'Chains' painted on it and the number '986' in the corner.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a series of works from the Black Fella's Dreaming Gallery purchased by the Museum in 2009. It includes one painting each by Yondee (Shane Howard), Gordon Hookey, and Adam Hill and nine works by Gordon Syron, both painter and founder and sole collector of the Gallery. Gordon and his partner Elaine Syron continue to own the remainder of works collected for the Gallery, and advocate for a permanent "keeping place" to house this unique collection of over 400 contemporary Aboriginal artworks gathered over the past four decades. 

The importance of this collection lies in its alternative view of Australian history and society, re-owned and re-painted by Aboriginal artists who express a savage and satirical commentary on issues ranging from "invasion" to land rights, alcoholism, custody, racism and the Church. The sense of injustice is tempered by the humour used in expressing such opinions, with some of the works allowing the visitor to actively engage in a transfer of roles of Aboriginal people and the viewer, like Syron's own 'The Black Bastards Are Coming no. 3', reversing the roles of first contact.
records.source_copyright: Copyright National Museum of Australia / CC BY-NC

The mission was established after Yass residents put pressure on authorities to remove the Aboriginal people camped near the proposed site of the town waterworks and, more generally, to remove them from the town. Hollywood Mission was located on the edge of the town, out of sight, and on the top of a stony hill, exposed to the westerly winds. It is remembered as one of the coldest places in Yass. The mission houses were two-roomed structures, made of corrugated iron positioned and on concrete stumps. Over the years, their front and back verandahs tended to be filled in to make extra rooms.

Household objects like this are important because very few pieces of material culture from Hollywood Mission survive.
records.physical_description: A rusted metal spoon with one side bent inwardly out of shape. The spoon is curved at the end of the handle.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of a metal fork and spoon, the fragments of five small glass bottles and a glass bottle stopper. Eric Bell OAM, elder of the Ngunnawal (Wallabaloa) nation, found these objects on the site of the former Hollywood Aboriginal Reserve, often referred to as Hollywood Mission, on the outskirts of Yass in south-western New South Wales. He spent his childhood and early adulthood on Hollywood Mission and his memories of life on the mission are amongst only a handful that are recorded. Eric Bell considered it very important that the history of the reserve be remembered, both as part of the history of Aboriginal people of that area and as part of the history of the township of Yass.

During the first half of the 20th century, many Aboriginal people lived on church or government run missions. Hollywood Mission opened in 1934 following pressure from the residents of Yass to remove Aboriginal people from the township. The mission was located on the edge of Yass, overlooking the cemetery and slaughter yard. It was positioned on the top of a stony hill, exposed to westerly winds. The soil was generally too poor to grow vegetables and the water supply was always inadequate. The mission was progressively closed from the early 1950s. It was deserted by 1960. Today, evidence of Hollywood Mission has been destroyed and the area is now private property.

records.title: Tasmanian Aboriginal bark canoe
places: Launceston, Tasmania, Australia (Place made)
records.physical_description: A canoe made from strips of light coloured bark overlapping each other and held together with strips of bark wound around the many layers. The canoe has rounded edges and a curved floor and base. Some of the strips holding the canoe together are coming loose. There are a number of metal nails and pins along the sides.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a Tasmanian bark canoe made by Rex Greeno. It is 4.7 metres long and has a clay pan at one end containing charcoal, and has five propelling poles.  The collection also includes a sample of the bark used to make the canoe.

Rex Greeno was born on Flinders Island in Bass Strait. His mother was Dulcie Greeno, a noted Tasmanian Aboriginal shell necklace maker whose work is also represented in the Museum's National Historical Collection. His grandfather Silas Mansell taught him mutton-birding, kangaroo and wallaby snaring, and making craypots and boats. A fisherman like his father, Greeno was inspired to make traditional Tasmanian paper bark canoes, after researching late eighteenth and early nineteenth century accounts by maritime explorers and other early European settlers to the island. He made this canoe with his son Dean and grandson Harrison, thus passing on these traditional skills to a new generation. Paperbark canoes have not been seen in Tasmania since the early nineteenth century. A few model canoes from the nineteenth century made by Aboriginal people, survive in a few museum collections. This is the fifth canoe that Greeno has constructed and was commissioned for the National Museum of Australia.

records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Aurukun Christmas card featuring Missionary's son and Aboriginal Head Stockman's son (1960s)
places: Aurukun, Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, Australia (Place depicted)
records.description:
Sold by Deaconess Winifred Hilliard to Janet Norris.
Christmas card from Aurukun featuring Missionary's son and Aboriginal Head Stockman's son (1960s).
records.physical_description: A Christmas card made of white glossy cardboard featuring a photograph on the front depicting two boys in shorts, smiling and looking to one side in front of a sky of dark clouds. Black text printed inside the card reads 'Sons of Australia / Missionary's Son and Aboriginal Head / Stockman's Son, friends at Aurukun, / Northern Queensland' and 'And lo! From the heaven above, / An angel leaned from the glory, / ...' in two columns on the left side and 'CHRISTMAS AND NEW YEAR GREETINGS / from' on the right side.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises arts and crafts sold by the late Deaconess Winifred Hilliard to Janet Norris, a fellow member of the Trinity Presbyterian Church, Camberwell. Winifred maintained a craft program at Ernabella Mission from the 1950s when Janet was a member of the Presbyterian Women’s Missionary Union at Trinity. The role of the group was to raise money to fund craft activities and support the various missions. They did this by selling Christmas cards and items made by the Aboriginal peoples of Ernabella, in particular.

As a collection, these items represent the diversity of arts and crafts produced at such missions during the 1950s and 1960s. In addition to colourful Christmas cards, featuring reproductions of rock art, photographs of Aboriginal families, and abstract designs in Ernabella style, the collection contains two 'walka' paintings used for Christmas card designs and four examples of pokerwork from Ernabella. The collection also includes an early example of a batik by Tjunkaya Tayapa. These items reflect the Norris family’s strong support for the mission at Ernabella and other Presbyterian missions, as well as the reach of Winifred’s work in promoting Ernabella arts and crafts over the decades she lived there.

records.physical_description: Printed cardboard packet used to hold 8 "Western Australian Aboriginal Sport Stars" trading cards, namely; "Syripa, Karl, Krishelle, Mark, Cheryl, Joey, Nova, Brendan." whose portrait shots appear on the front of the pocket with their names underneath and the words "Smoking Sux" at the bottom of the packet
records.significance_statement:
The 'Health Department of Western Australia' collection consists of sixteen anti-smoking sports trading cards features eight Aboriginal sport stars from Western Australia: Nova Peris, Syripa Macer, Brendon Rodoreda, Joey Smith, Krishelle Mitchell, Karl Feifar, Cheryl Kickett Tucker and Mark Chalker.

In 1994 the Aboriginal Social Justice Task Force report recognised youth smoking as an issue of concern. The Smoking and Health Program developed the Aboriginal Sport Star Swap Cards, capitalising on the swap card craze. The cards promoted a health message by using young, positive Aboriginal sports people as role models. The cards are proving an effective way of promoting better health among Aboriginal youth in Western Australia.

records.title: The Hon Robert Tickner MP...Rebutting the Myths Some facts about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs
places: Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, Australia (Place of publication)
records.physical_description: Seven A4 pages stapled in the top left corner. Text on the front page reads in part "The Hon Robert Tickner MP...Rebutting the Myths Some facts about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs...". The booklet was produced in July 1992 and has typed text in black ink on both sides of the paper.
records.significance_statement:
A collection of Aboriginal protest material relating to south-eastern Australia.  These objects have a two-fold cultural context. First is their association with important issues in relation to Aboriginal rights, particularly land rights. The other is their association with Terry Fox, who in his own words was "a white activist" giving Kooris, particularly on the New South Wales south coast, assistance in their struggles for their rights.

The objects like posters and the T-shirt are the material expressions behind complex social justice issues like land rights. They state very succinctly what the issue or campaign is about. The book is a collection of land rights claims made in NSW in the 1970s. Each case explains what is being sought and the reasons why. The papers and documents look at different issues, for example Native.Title, in more depth and give comment on these issues from Aboriginal viewpoints. Often these issues produce little else in the way of material objects other than paperwork like correspondence and minutes from meetings. All of these objects were acquired by Teny Fox during his involvement with Koori communities, either when he was assisting with particular protests for land rights or working for communities such as Wallaga Lake.

records.title: 66 Vexillidae Vexillum Jukesi shells
places: Minjilang, Croker Island, Northern Territory, Australia (Place collected)
records.description:
The Lady Helen Blackburn collection features more than five hundred seashells from Australian beaches, reefs and islands.

Lady Helen Blackburn was born Bryony Helen Dutton in 1918, the third of four children to a pioneering pastoralist family. She grew up on the historic Anlaby Station near Kapunda (the oldest stud sheep station in South Australia) and formed a close relationship with her younger brother Geoffrey Dutton, who would become a celebrated poet, novelist and historian. The Dutton family spent summers at Rocky Point, the beloved family holiday home on the north coast of Kangaroo Island, where Helen's curiosity and love of nature led to a passion for shell collecting that would last a lifetime.

In 1951, Helen married lawyer Richard Blackburn (later Sir Richard). They lived in Adelaide and started a family. Rocky Point remained a focal holiday destination, and Helen's passion for shell collecting continued to thrive. "Shell collecting has been my greatest joy in life", she later wrote. "Just walking on a good beach, hoping to find beach specimens has made me as happy as hunting for live specimens." (Lady Helen Blackburn collection file: National Museum of Australia).
    
In 1966, Richard was appointed resident judge of the Supreme Court of the Northern Territory, where he presided over the first Aboriginal land rights case heard in an Australian court: Milirrpum v Nabalco (1971). During her time in the Northern Territory, Helen pursued her passion for collecting shells. She visited the Gove Peninsula of Arnhem Land (the country of the Yolngu people of Yirrkala) with her husband, and took the opportunity to search for shells.

Such was her skill and reputation for shell collecting, that she did so on behalf of several major institutions, including the Australian, Darwin, Tasmanian and Western Australian Museums, the CSIRO and the University of New South Wales. Helen corresponded regularly with other shell collectors around the world, exchanging information and swapping shells to build up her collection. Her malacological knowledge, moreover, was such that she wrote a book on the, "Marine shells of the Darwin area". One of the shells she presented to the Australian Museum had never before been described, and now carries her name: Cryptomya blackburnae.

records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.title: Child's drawing - Games. Aboriginal children used the things around them by Craig Sturgeon, Shayne McLeod and Allyson
places: Jervis Bay School, Jervis Bay Village, Australian Capital Territory, Australia (Place created)
records.description:
This artwork is one of a series of some 3383 drawings and paintings on paper made between 1975-1977 by Aboriginal children from 70 schools across Australia. 

These artworks were collected by the Aboriginal Arts Board for potential use in 'The Aboriginal Children's History of Australia: Written and Illustrated by Australia's Aboriginal Children'. The book was published by Rigby, Adelaide in 1977. 

According to Robert Edwards, then Director of the Aboriginal Arts Board, the idea for collecting these Aboriginal Children's drawings evolved during a 1975 flight to Canberra. Serendipitously, Edwards sat next to Edward J. McGrath Jr, Director of the Hawaiian publishing firm, Island Heritage Limited. 

McGrath asked Edwards 'What do you do?' On hearing about the Aboriginal Arts Board's work with Australian Aboriginal communities, McGrath explained that he was publishing a series of Children's histories from different nations throughout the world. He produced from his briefcase a copy of 'A Child's History of Hawaii' and an exchange of ideas for a history book by Aboriginal children ensued. 

Edwards recalls that the flight was fortuitous, as he had been thinking about how to link Indigenous children into the Aboriginal Arts Board's art programs. Children's art seemed an obvious way of involving children, especially if the project could be organised through the school system.

A project to produce Children's artworks for a history book authored by Aboriginal children was subsequently proposed to the Aboriginal Arts Board, who approved and implemented the project in 1976.

Michael Gray was responsible for researching and coordinating the project, which incorporated 70 participating Aboriginal schools from all parts of Australia except Victoria and the Torres Strait.

The Aboriginal Arts Board transferred the collection of artworks to the National Museum of Australia in 1991.

records.title: Breastplate presented to Coomee Nullanga of Ulladulla NSW by Edmund Milne in 1909
places: New South Wales, Australia (Place made)
Murramarang, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)

records.description: Edmund Milne (1861-1917) was born in England and emigrated to Queensland with his parents 19 months later. He had had personal contact with Aboriginal people throughout his life, from when he was a small boy in Queensland and, from the late 1860s, in New South Wales. This contact may have led him to recording the names of Aboriginal people associated with particular objects in his collection, at a time when this was rarely done. Milne seems to have begun actively collecting Indigenous artefacts in the early 1880s and was still acquiring objects a few months before his death in 1917. His work with the NSW Railways (1876-1917) enabled him to meet a broad range of people who facilitated his collecting and associated activities like visiting Aboriginal sites. From at least the time he lived at Orange NSW (1906-1915), and later at Ryde (1915-1917), near to Sydney city, he displayed his collection at his home. In addition to a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts, Milne's collection included artefacts from the South Pacific and prehistoric implements from Egypt, France and England. In his will dated 12 December 1916, Milne bequeathed his “Anthropological collection” to the “first Federal Museum opened in the Federal Capital”. The collection remained at Ryde until early 1931 when it was acquired by the Australian Institute of Anatomy in Canberra. It remained there until the Institute's collections were transferred to the National Museum of Australia in 1985.

The man is laughing with his mouth open and is looking off to his right. There is one split in the background, and many splits in the frame on the left hand side. The second panel depicts the bust of an Aboriginal woman wearing a scarf around her head which is made from a different wood and varnished. records.title: Plastic-coated calico coaster printed with an Aboriginal-inspired motif, made by Annan Fabrics, Sydney
places: Mosman, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia (Place made)
Mosman, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia (Unspecified relationship)
records.physical_description: Plastic-coated calico coaster coated printed with an Aboriginal-inspired motif in white, red and black, on a light brown background.
records.significance_statement:
The 'Wal Beckhouse collection' consists of a calico tablecloth, rayon pillowcase and a plastic-coated coaster designed and manufactured by Annan Fabrics, a prolific silk-screen printers workshop operating in Mosman, Sydney between 1941 and 1954. The tablecloth depicts one of Annan Fabrics' most popular designs - 'Emu Track', a blue and grey design overlaid with interlocking emu footprints - and the pillowcase and coaster demonstrate other Aboriginal and floral-inspired designs typical of the company. The collection was acquired for the National Historical Collection in 1992 from Mr Wal Beckhouse (dates unknown), a former employee of Annan Fabrics between 1951 and 1953.  

Representative of the arts and crafts movement of the 1940s and early 1950s, these vivid designs are a testament to the entrepreneurship of artists Alexandra 'Nance' Kirkwood, (née Mackenzie) (1912-1999) and Anne Outlaw (1891-1991). The designs drew almost exclusively from Australian flora and fauna and, in response to interests of the time, adapted Aboriginal motifs and themes. As used to denote an authentic and recognisable Australian identity, Annan Fabrics received many commissions from corporate and private clients. Illustrative of the wider contextual use of Annan Fabrics' designs on a range of decorative arts, souvenirs and homewares, this collection allows researchers to explore issues of Australian identity, the use of Aboriginal motifs in decorative arts and conveys insight into Sydney-based artistic expression during the mid twentieth-century.

places: Blackstone (Papulankutja Aboriginal community), Western Australia, Australia (Place made)
Canberra, Australian Capital Territory, Australia (Place of event)
records.description:
The Seven Sisters Songline travels from the west to the east across the far western and central deserts. The sisters are pursued by a man, Yurla, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. Yurla becomes besotted by one of the sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. 

In the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands the lustful man Yurla is known as Wati Nyiru, and the Seven Sisters — the Minyipuru — become the Kungkarangkalpa. Pursuing the sisters with obsessive dedication, southwards from Irawa Bore, Wati Nyiru reveals his conflicted character in a moment of self-realisation at Walinynga (Cave Hill), where he no longer recognises his own footprint. Here, as elsewhere, knowledge is transmitted in old and new ways. Inma, or performance, is the primary mode of knowledge transfer and holds the old traditions secure; and through ceramics the elders have found an imaginative way of representing both the Seven Sisters and the bush food into which Wati Nyiru transforms himself.   (Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p67)

This part of the songline begins at Irawa Bore near Wallara in the north, and extends to Alkara in South Australia. At the distinctive flat-topped mountain of Atila (Mount Conner), the sisters see Nyiru spying on them. They flee south to Witapula waterhole where they sing and splash. Frightened by Nyiru's sudden appearance, the sisters disappear underground and follow the subterranean waterways, surfacing at No. 3 Bore. But Nyiru is waiting for them, and they run south, past Mulga Park to Walinynga, where they build a spinifex shelter known today as Cave Hill. It is here that Wati Nyiru, hoping to approach the sisters 'proper way', attempts to control his desire by wrapping his excited member around his waist like a belt. But lust overcomes him, and the sisters escape from
the shelter through a small opening at the rear, and dance southwards past Kuli into other lands. (Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p87)

records.description:
This artwork is one of a series of some 3383 drawings and paintings on paper made between 1975-1977 by Aboriginal children from 70 schools across Australia. 

These artworks were collected by the Aboriginal Arts Board for potential use in 'The Aboriginal Children's History of Australia: Written and Illustrated by Australia's Aboriginal Children'. The book was published by Rigby, Adelaide in 1977. 

According to Robert Edwards, then Director of the Aboriginal Arts Board, the idea for collecting these Aboriginal Children's drawings evolved during a 1975 flight to Canberra. Serendipitously, Edwards sat next to Edward J. McGrath Jr, Director of the Hawaiian publishing firm, Island Heritage Limited. 

McGrath asked Edwards 'What do you do?' On hearing about the Aboriginal Arts Board's work with Australian Aboriginal communities, McGrath explained that he was publishing a series of Children's histories from different nations throughout the world. He produced from his briefcase a copy of 'A Child's History of Hawaii' and an exchange of ideas for a history book by Aboriginal children ensued. 

Edwards recalls that the flight was fortuitous, as he had been thinking about how to link Indigenous children into the Aboriginal Arts Board's art programs. Children's art seemed an obvious way of involving children, especially if the project could be organised through the school system.

A project to produce Children's artworks for a history book authored by Aboriginal children was subsequently proposed to the Aboriginal Arts Board, who approved and implemented the project in 1976.

Michael Gray was responsible for researching and coordinating the project, which incorporated 70 participating Aboriginal schools from all parts of Australia except Victoria and the Torres Strait.

The Aboriginal Arts Board transferred the collection of artworks to the National Museum of Australia in 1991.
records.physical_description: Two male figures walk towards a female figure with a stick who stands close to a shelter. Artist: Regina Butts, 13yrs.

records.description: Edmund Milne (1861-1917) was born in England and emigrated to Queensland with his parents 19 months later. He had had personal contact with Aboriginal people throughout his life, from when he was a small boy in Queensland and, from the late 1860s, in New South Wales. This contact may have led him to recording the names of Aboriginal people associated with particular objects in his collection, at a time when this was rarely done. Milne seems to have begun actively collecting Indigenous artefacts in the early 1880s and was still acquiring objects a few months before his death in 1917. His work with the NSW Railways (1876-1917) enabled him to meet a broad range of people who facilitated his collecting and associated activities like visiting Aboriginal sites. From at least the time he lived at Orange NSW (1906-1915), and later at Ryde (1915-1917), near to Sydney city, he displayed his collection at his home. In addition to a large collection of Aboriginal artefacts, Milne's collection included artefacts from the South Pacific and prehistoric implements from Egypt, France and England. In his will dated 12 December 1916, Milne bequeathed his “Anthropological collection” to the “first Federal Museum opened in the Federal Capital”. The collection remained at Ryde until early 1931 when it was acquired by the Australian Institute of Anatomy in Canberra. It remained there until the Institute's collections were transferred to the National Museum of Australia in 1985.
records.physical_description: A crescent shaped brass breastplate with a hole at the edge of each horn to attach a chain. Engraved on the anterior surface is 'BILLY KELLY / KING OF / BROADWATER'. records.title: 'Kungkarrangkalpa Tjurkurpa' 2015, by Anawari Inpiti Mitchell, Angilyiya Tjapiti Mitchell, Lalla West, Jennifer Nginyaka Mitchell, Eileen Tjayanka Woods,
places: Blackstone (Papulankutja Aboriginal community), Western Australia, Australia (Place created)
Kuru Ala, Papulankutja, Western Australia, Australia (Place created)
records.description:
This is a ollaborative painting made by Anawari Inpiti Mitchell; Angilyiya Tjapitji Mitchell; Lalla West, Jennifer Nginyaka Mitchell; Eileen Tjayanka Woods, Lesley Laidlaw and Robert Woods at Kuru Ala.

The Seven Sisters Songline travels from the west to the east across the far western and central deserts. The sisters are pursued by a man, Yurla in the west and Wati Nyiru further east, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by one of the sisters and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. Today, this saga is visible in the Orion constellation and Pleiades star cluster as a constant reminder of the consequences of attempting to possess something through wrongful means. 

"When the songline reaches the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, the tone darkens and the actions of Wati Nyiru become more sinister. His obsession with the eldest sister is the major theme, and the paintings acquired relating to the Seven Sisters focus on several key events — the capture of the eldest sister, the cooking and eating of kuniya, (the carpet snake, which is a manifestation of the shape-shifter), and the transformation of the sisters into  stars. 
On the Ngaanyatjarra Lands, people are connected to sites through their kinship to the Ancestral characters who inhabit the narrative. The rituals of dance and song — inma — enact the universal meanings of the Tjukurrpa. The Seven Sisters drama unfolds along two songlines in this section. As you journey along the Kuru Ala songline to the south and Wanarn to the north. the paintings function as portals to place."
(Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017, p119)

"Kungkarrangkalpa Tjukurrpa was painted on site at Kuru Ala in 2013, on the occasion of a re-enactment of the Kuru Ala story. Each of the participants  painted the section of the story and country for which they had responsibility, arranging themselves in relation to the most senior custodian, Eileen  Tjayanka Woods. To collaborate on such a significant story requires everyone to know what they can and can't tell, and assumes a precise knowledge of how all the parts fit together: those parts comprising kinship, country and story. Although the painting was supervised silently by 'bosses', people painted without discussion. Tjayanka Woods, whose knowledge of the site was undisputed, painted Wati Nyiru. Robert Muntantji Woods, boss of the men's story, painted the carpet snake. Tjayanka's 'daughters' painted the capture of the  snake and the healing site. Lalla West and Lesley Laidlaw painted the disposal and flight of the snake that appeared as a  rainbow at Kulyuru, the next site of the drama." (Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, NMA Press, 2017)
records.physical_description: An acrylic dot painting on a square canvas featuring several concentric circles in the top left corner and along the top. The lower right corner features eight human figures. To the left of the figures and about a third of the way up the painting there is a light pink section that has many human foot prints. There are several 'U' shapes around the canvas. The background is dots of various colours including green, brown, white, orange, pink, blue and yellow.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises two acrylic paintings on canvas created by artists from the Papulankutja (Blackstone) Aboriginal community in Western Australia. 'Kungkarrangkalpa Tjurkurpa', 2015 is a collaborative work by Anawari Inpiti Mitchell, Angilyiya Tjapitji Mitchell, Lalla West, Jennifer Nginyaka Mitchell, Eileen Tjayanka Woods, Lesley Laidlaw and Robert Woods. 'Kungkarrangkalpa   Seven Sisters' 2015, is by Angilyiya Tjapitji Mitchell. Mrs Woods, Jennifer Nginyaka Mitchell, Anawari Inpiti Mitchell and Angilyiya Tjapitji Mitchell are Senior Custodians of the Kungkarangkalpa (Seven Sisters) Songline at the important site, Kuru Ala.  

The Kungkarrangkalpa (Seven Sisters) songline travels from the west to the east across the far western and central deserts. In the story the sisters are pursued by an old man, Wati Nyiru, who is a shape shifter with transformative powers. He becomes besotted by the older sister in particular and pursues them endlessly in order to possess them. The two works in this collection represent different aspects of the Seven Sisters story related to Kuru Ala. In 'Kungkarrangkalpa Tjurkurpa' the artists have documented several aspect of the events that happened during the Seven Sisters’ visit to Kuru Ala and their journey to Kulyuru. 'Kungkarrangkalpa   Seven Sisters' illustrates a more detailed narrative about the activities of the Seven Sister’s at Kuru Ala. Angilyiya Tjapitji Mitchell has painted blue circles all around the work representing the digging holes where the sisters were looking for kunia (carpet snake) into which Wati Nyiru transformed his phallus. Nyiru is identifiable as u-shapes singing on either side of the sisters, with his spear and spear thrower. The ladies feed of what they think is kunia and get very sick. They are pictured staggering in groups around kunia in the centre. Then they ascend into the sky, as shown in the top part of the painting.

Ivanhoe, New South Wales, Australia (Associated place)
records.description: Made in the traditional way of Aboriginal people of the Ivanhoe District of New South Wales.
records.physical_description: Bag woven in acrylic and wool yarn in bands of green, black, yellow, red and white.
records.significance_statement:
The Eliza Kennedy collection comprises a woven bag and a sample of weaving, both in wool.

The bag was woven by Mrs Eliza Kennedy, a Nyiampaa woman, in mid March 1992 at her home in Albury NSW.  The weaving sample, which shows how to commence the weaving and how to continue onto the next row, was done largely by Mrs Kennedy but partly by National Museum curator David Kaus who was shown the process by Mrs Kennedy. South-eastern Australian woven bags, used by both men and women, are rare in museum collections. Mrs Kennedy may have been one of the last people in central NSW to have been taught how to make this form of netted bag. Previously, they would have been made of vegetable fibre but when she learnt to make them, they were made by extracting strands from blankets. The availability of wool provides a ready-made medium for this kind of work.

records.title: Coolamon with Aboriginal figure by William Ricketts
places: Mount Dandenong, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia (Place made)
records.description: Artist and potter Williams Ricketts (1898–1993) was inspired by the spirituality and dignity of Aboriginal people and wanted to draw attention to what he saw as their connection to the environment. The sculptures he produced at his Mt. Dandenong pottery feature Aboriginal and mythical figures, Australian birds, animals and hybrid creatures, some appearing to emerge from the organic forms of trees and rocks, with larger works designed to blend into the native garden settings where he displayed them. His domestic ware, like much Australian studio pottery of the time, is decorated with Aboriginal figures, flora and fauna. Coolamons, probably cast and hand finished, were a popular form made by Ricketts.
records.physical_description: An earthenware coolamon modelled and glazed to look like a hollowed log with relief decoration of an Aboriginal face to one side of the handle.
records.significance_statement:
This collection comprises a range of items associated with Winifred Hilliard and the Ernabella Aboriginal community in Central Australia. It includes art and craft items, film equipment, a camera and other items used by Hilliard in her work as an arts advisor with Aboriginal people at Ernabella, as well as her photograph albums, awards and items relating to her involvement in the Presbyterian and later Uniting Church. Collectively, it is representative of Hilliard's adult life, particularly at Ernabella.

Winifred Hilliard was a Presbyterian and later Uniting Church deaconess who, from 1954 until her retirement in 1986, worked as arts advisor in the Ernabella art centre. Hilliard and her work with the community contributed  to the development of the Aboriginal arts and craft industry in central Australia. Established in 1948, Ernabella Arts is one of the longest continually running Aboriginal art centres in Australia and is noted for the range of items produced there. It was at Ernabella that the first batiks were produced by Aboriginal artists in the early 1970s, with artists from Ernabella teaching the technique to Indigenous artists in other communities. Hilliard was influential in introducing new art forms at Ernabella and it was Hilliard who suggested Ernabella artists try batik. This brought them national and international recognition from the 1970s for several decades. This collection highlights the contribution of Hilliard and the artists in making Ernabella a key organisation in the development of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art industry.
records.acknowledgement: Donated by Winifred, Susan and Grant Hilliard

records.physical_description: An earthenware plaque with relief decoration of the head of an Aboriginal child, partly glazed.
records.significance_statement:
The William Ricketts Sculpture Collection consists of  Lot 013, a relief plaque of an Aboriginal boy and Lot 014, a wall plaque of a head of an Aboriginal elder of the Dreamtime. Both in good condition.

William Ricketts (1899 - 1993) is an internationally renowned Australian sculpture whose concern for the environment and Aboriginal people was the major inspiration for his work.  Rickett's sculptures of Aboriginal mythology allowed him to express his convictions and beliefs through this medium.  The two reliefs of Aboriginal children are examples of the type of work produced by Ricketts during his lifetime, particularly during his time spent with the Pitjantjara and Arrente people of Central Australia.

records.description: Artist statement: The Aboriginal Embassy site outside Old Parliament House, Canberra, should be listed as part of the National Estate because of its importance to the Indigenous peoples of Australia. It represents our survival and triumph over over injustice, and the unity it forged amongst our people. (Art of Place: Second National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander HeritageArt Award and Exhibition. 1994)

places: Mount Dandenong, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia (Place made)
records.description: Artist and potter Williams Ricketts (1898–1993) was inspired by the spirituality and dignity of Aboriginal people and wanted to draw attention to what he saw as their connection to the environment. The sculptures he produced at his Mt. Dandenong pottery feature Aboriginal and mythical figures, Australian birds, animals and hybrid creatures, some appearing to emerge from the organic forms of trees and rocks, with larger works designed to blend into the native garden settings where he displayed them.
records.physical_description: An earthenware plaque with relief decoration of the head of a man with a long beard partly, glazed. There is a small hole in the top for hanging. Incised on reverse 'Wm Ricketts', with green felt attached to base.
records.significance_statement:
This collection consists of two William Ricketts reliefs of Aboriginal children.  Lot 113 is a sculpture of an Aboriginal child looking to the left, signed on the reverse.  Lot 115 is a terracotta relief of an Aboriginal child's face.  They are in good condition.

William Ricketts is an internationally renowned Australian sculpture whose concern for the environment and Aboriginal people was the major inspiration for his work.  Rickett's sculptures of Aboriginal mythology allowed him to express his convictions and beliefs through this medium.  The two reliefs of Aboriginal children are examples of the type of work produced by Ricketts during his lifetime, particularly during his time spent with the Pitjantjara and Arrente people of Central Australia.

The prints are black and are of a left and a right hand, and  are located at the bottom of the painting. At the top of the painting is a red face like image with a oval like shape above it. records.significance_statement:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs Art collection comprises 2050 artworks and other objects.  The artworks - which numerically dominate the collection - were produced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities throughout Australia. The accumulation of these artworks into a single collection has resulted from the choices and selections made during a 38 year period by a variety of staff working for the Council for Aboriginal Affairs (CAA), the Department of Aboriginal Affairs (DAA), the Aboriginal Development Commission (ADC) and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission (ATSIC) at the national, regional and local levels.

The collection spans the years following the 1967 referendum, when dramatic changes in the governance of Aboriginal people took place, up to 2005 when the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission was dissolved. It provides a snapshot of the diversity and changes in Indigenous art and its representation which occurred during the period of its formation. The small number of 'non-art' objects in the collection is also significant in providing insights into the working of the various Commonwealth bodies involved in Indigenous affairs. As well as the significance of many of the individual pieces, the collection is also significant as a whole, as a complex artefact stemming from Australia's history of governance of Australian Indigenous peoples.

records.physical_description: A poster of an Australian Aboriginal cricket team mounted in a glazed, rectangular, dark brown wooden frame. It depicts sixteen oval-shaped individually named photographic portrait images of the cricketers surrounded by a gold coloured oval border. 'AUSTRALIAN' is in a narrow banner printed across the top, above the oval, and two smaller banners flank a crude representation of the Australian coat-of-arms, with the motto 'ADVANCE AUSTRALIA', below it. One of the small banners contains 'ABORIGINAL' and the other 'CRICKETERS'. 'Photographed by P. DAWSON, Hamilton, Victoria / REGISTERED' is printed in the border of the oval at the bottom. A newspaper clipping taped to the back of the frame is titled 'ABORIGINAL TEAM OF 1868'.
records.significance_statement:
The Bruce Gillam Collection comprises an Aboriginal boomerang and a timber-framed montage of photographs of the cricket team selected to tour England in 1868. The boomerang is typical of those made by Aboriginal people in the region around northwest New South Wales in the mid-19th century. The photographic montage is one of many created by Peter Dawson of Hamilton in Victoria to promote the 1868 tour. 

The touring cricket team of 1868 comprised thirteen Aboriginal players captained by the ex-English player Charles Lawrence. The team performed well on the long and arduous tour, winning 14 and drawing 19 of the 47 games they played. Despite this success, however, only two of the team were to play representative cricket on their return, and then only briefly.

records.description: Narmoola Pool is one of a series of waterholes, creeks, lakes and drainages formed by Wonarmbi, the water snake of the Guwarra people of the Western Desert, north of Leonora, Western Australia. Wonarmbi came from the desert through Bandya to Cundeelee where it travelled to the sea. Wonarmbi still resides in the waterholes, including Narmoola Pool, along the route of its travels. Any damage to the pool will cause the serpent to leave and the water to dry up. Wonarmbi is not dangerous to people and children can swim safely in the pool. When the ablutions Wiltja was built at Corringie the story of Wonarmbi was painted on the structure. The painting depicts the waterholes as the life source of the desert, the people, and the reptiles. On top of the structure, five people are depicted camping at Narmoola Pool. The story protects the structure in the same way that it protects Narmoola Pool. This is a scale model of the larger structure that was built at Corringie near Leonora, which was being considered in 1995 as a prototype for housing in remote Western Australian communities.
